utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, please start.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before we continue with the questions, I'd like to provide a document which Professor Rakic in the meantime managed to come by from Belgrade. It is the Official Gazette of the SFRY, and I'd like to ask the usher to place it on the overhead projector because it's one copy and that will enable the witness to read it, and I'll be able to follow. Mr. Bonomy was interested in whether a document existed with respect to the establishment of the imminent threat of war in the SFRY, and it related to the session of the 1st of October. I hope you have it on the overhead projector now.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: May we see it on the overhead projector?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We've got it there now, but it's rather illegible.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But you can read it from the actual document, from the paper, not on the screen. It's very short. I can read it on my copy. Can you read it?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What does it say?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "On the basis of Article 316, paragraph 1 of the constitution of the SFRY and Article 6 of the law on total national defence, the Official Gazette of the SFRY, number 21/82 and 35/91, the Presidency of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, at its session held on the 1st of October, 1991, in assessing the current political and security situation in the country, determined --"

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And what does it say then?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "... determined the existence of an imminent threat of war in the SFRY. This Act will be published in the Official Gazette of the SFRY, which is the Official Gazette.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Read out the decision to the end. What does it say? What's the number?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "190, 1st of October, 1991, Belgrade, the Vice-president Dr. Branko Kostic in his own hand."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So we're dealing there with the 1st of October, and that's what you were testifying about, and this document was published at the time in the Official Gazette, establishing that the Presidency had found that there was the imminent threat of war in the country. That's the document.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That is it. But I forgot that it was published in the Official Gazette. But we were discussing whether it was a decision proper or whether it was some sort of assessment or appraisal. I said that there need not have been a decision but that that was the general evaluation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Well, we clarified that now on the basis of the document.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, Mr. Robinson, the document is a short one. It's not translated, but the witness has just read it out and it's been translated, so I'd like to tender it into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: The Prosecution has also looked for this document, and actually it's already an exhibit. It's Exhibit 526, tab 28.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: That's the same document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. Milosevic. There's no need to ...

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will have to verify and see if this is the same document. I don't remember it ever having been tendered here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Professor Kostic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It came -- came into evidence through Professor Ivan Kristan. That information is from Judge Kwon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Last time you left off explaining what kind of resistance there was with respect to the adoption of the Vance Plan. Did you personally take part in trying to convince the leadership in Krajina to accept the plan?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I did take part, and very intensively. Not only I myself but the overall Presidency of the SFRY, all the members who advocated the Yugoslav federalist option. And at the beginning, we had two very long meetings - they lasted for six hours - with the whole leadership of the Republic of Srpska Krajina. And when we considered that we had gained their acquiescence, their agreement, it turned out that despite Mr. Milan Babic's promises that he would accept the Vance Plan, despite all of the reservations he had, he did promise that he would make a public statement to the information media to that effect, that remained at the level of promises. Mr. Babic never did that. And at the Convention on Yugoslavia held on the 3rd of January, 1992, the president of the Assembly of the Republic of Srpska Krajina fiercely attacked the Yugoslav state Presidency because of the Vance Plan, accusing us of betraying the interests of the Serbs in Krajina. And after that, we had a marathon meeting which went on for 40 hours, with interruptions, and I said that at that meeting, in addition to the members of the Yugoslav state Presidency, we had the participation of the most responsible representatives of Serbia, Montenegro, federal institutions, and the Supreme Command Staff as well, as well as the federal Assembly, representatives of the leadership of the Serb people in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and not only the government of the Republic of Srpska Krajina and the president of the Republika Srpska Krajina Milan Babic, but also all the presidents of the municipalities --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Professor, please remember, short answers, and just an answer that is sufficient. There is no need for that level of detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So briefly, there was the leadership of Krajina there and the leadership of Yugoslavia; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Attending that meeting.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And that's the meeting that went on for 40 hours?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And what was the purpose of that meeting?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The purpose of that meeting was, to all intents and purposes, to reach an agreement, because we had agreed with everybody else that Mr. Milan Babic had been -- should be persuaded to accept the plan, because we as the Yugoslav state Presidency weren't able to inform either Mr. Cyrus Vance or the Secretary-General of the United Nations, Mr. Boutros-Ghali about the acceptance of the Vance Plan until we had reached agreement with the leadership of the Serb people in Krajina. And since we didn't have that agreement and couldn't get it at that meeting with Mr. Babic, we decided to organise an Assembly session of the Republic of Srpska Krajina in Glina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And was that session organised?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The question was simply what was the purpose of that meeting. Just answer the question. You've already answered it. Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you didn't manage to convince Babic at that meeting, and you convened an Assembly meeting in Glina; right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You went to Glina to attend the Assembly meeting, did you? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: At whose request did you go to Glina?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At your own personal request, and that was the only time you addressed us directly during that period of time, the year that I spent in Belgrade. You rang me up on the phone and asked me --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. You've answered the question. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Just tell us the result of that Assembly session which you attended.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Assembly of the Republic of Srpska Krajina finally confirmed the signature of Milan Paspalj in Belgrade who, as president of the Assembly in the absence of the president of the republic, placed his signature on the Vance Plan, and it was only after that that we were in a situation as the Yugoslav state Presidency to inform the UN Secretary-General that Vance's plan had been adopted.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And what about the authorities in Croatia? How did they view the Vance Plan?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The authorities in Croatia had a very negative view of the Vance Plan and they put up great resistance because the Vance Plan guaranteed, finally, the establishment of a truce, which didn't suit the Croatian authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In tab 64, we have the Vance-Owen Plan. Could you find it, please. Have you found it?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What does point 1 of the Vance-Owen Plan provide for with respect to the overall object of the UN mission and its duration? Read it out.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Point 1 says: "A UN peace-keeping operation in Yugoslavia is envisaged as an interim arrangement to create the conditions for peace and security required for the negotiation of an overall settlement of the Yugoslav crisis. This operation should not prejudice the outcome of negotiations to this end."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please, what attitude of this aim of the mission to create conditions for peace and security required for the negotiation of an overall settlement of the Yugoslav crisis? So what was the -- what was that aim and goal on the part of the mission and the SFRY's aim?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They coincided completely, because we couldn't stop the fighting, the paramilitaries against the JNA especially in the Republic of Serb Krajina. We weren't able to achieve a truce.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And what was the relationship between that goal, that end, and the steps taken by the leadership of Serbia and myself?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, our attempts were the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What was the relationship of the secessionist republic's leadership with respect to an overall settlement of the Yugoslav crisis, which is mentioned there? What was their attitude towards that?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the leadership, especially in Slovenia and Croatia, didn't find that this concept suited their aims, nor did they wish to find an overall settlement to the Yugoslav crisis, especially not the leadership in Croatia, because the leadership in Croatia, there were -- was encouraged, especially by Germany and some other European countries, with respect to the threats they were hurling at us, and they kept saying that if the war conflicts did not cease, they would recognise Croatia's independence. We concluded so many truces and cease-fires, and they were all violated by Croatian paramilitaries, that there was nothing we could do at that point.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell us just briefly, please, what, to quote this area, what does it mean by the protected UN areas? What territory do those areas comprise?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: UNPAs meant areas with Serb majority population on the territory of Croatia, or alternatively, a large number of minority Serbs in places where, due to inter-ethnic conflict, the areas had turned into a crisis spot.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, tell us, what does this plan say? Which areas should become UNPAs? Point A.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Point A, it says these would be areas where, in the opinion of the Secretary-General, special interim arrangements would be necessary to ensure that lasting cease-fire is maintained. These would be areas in which Serbs constitute the majority or a substantial minority of the population and where inter-ethnic tensions have led to armed conflict in the recent past. As pointed out before, special arrangements in these areas would be temporary and would not prejudice the outcome of political negotiations towards an overall settlement of the Yugoslav crisis.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we see with the AV booth what is going on, because there is interference in the headphones, like a soundtrack or something.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The matter raised by Mr. Milosevic, I'd like to have that checked out by the technical people. It's being checked, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, could you please read item 7 of the Vance Plan.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Item 7: "The armed forces of the United Nations and police monitors would be deployed in various areas of Croatia, which would be called the United Nations Protected Areas (UNPA). These areas would be demilitarised. All the armed forces in these areas would have to either withdraw or be disbanded. The mandate of the United Nations troops would be to ensure that these areas remain demilitarised and that all the persons residing in these areas are protected from fear of armed attack. The role of the United Nations police monitors would be to ensure that the local police forces carry out their duties without discriminating between different ethnic groups and without violating anybody's human rights. To the extent that the United Nations forces take over their responsibilities in UNPAs, all JNA forces will be deployed in other populated areas in Croatia or outside that republic."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That's enough. You don't have to read about humanitarian agencies. So, Professor Kostic, if UNPAs, according to item 8, were in fact areas populated by Serbs, how are we to understand the sentence from item 7 that you've just read, which reads: "The role of the United Nations police monitors --" or, rather: "UNPAs should remain demilitarised so that all persons residing in these areas are protected from fear of armed attack"?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were crisis hotspots, these areas, and when we wrote to the United Nations Secretary-General and the Security Council, we advised them that our main wish is to deploy the troops in certain areas to protect the Serbian population that would enable us to withdraw the JNA from these areas. In other words, that UN troops should take over the role that the JNA had been performing that far.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What "fear of armed attack" is meant here?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's fear from armed attack by Croatian paramilitary units. We've discussed it already.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Before the UN peacekeepers arrived, were there such attacks?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were many such attacks by Croat paramilitary units, special police units, and so on and so forth. They were being sent to those areas where police stations already existed, but the problem for them was that those police stations were manned by the local people, a lot of them Serbs. And they wanted to disarm those local police forces that consisted of the local people, Serbs, and that combined with the fear of the Serbs, of seeing a repetition of World War II, led to conflicts. Roads were cut off, logs were placed across roads to prevent passage. That's why it was called the log revolution.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: It's -- after the UN peacekeepers arrived, were there violations of the Vance Plan?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, a number. There were armed attacks and raids. Moreover, in certain areas Croatian armed forces penetrated the UNPAs, although the Vance Plan envisaged not only UNPAs but also yellow areas that should also have been demilitarised, with Croat forces withdrawn and pulled back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Sorry, let me see if I understand this. You say that the -- the UN police monitors wanted to disarm the local police forces that consisted of local people, Serbs, and that led to conflicts. Is it your understanding of the Vance-Owen Plan that that was part of their role?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, there must be a misunderstanding due to misinterpretation. I didn't talk about police monitors of the UN. I said that there were attacks by Croatian paramilitaries, Croatian special police forces, and armed forces on the local population when, according to orders from their leadership, they tried to penetrate these areas populated by the majority Serb populace. Those areas also had police stations, like every other area in Croatia, with the difference that these police stations were manned and led by representatives of the Serb population. And the Croat authorities sent their armed forces to disarmed these --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. The impression was given that -- to me, at any rate, that it was the UN police monitors, but you have now explained it, yes. Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, maybe confusion occurred because when we quoted item 7, there is indeed reference to UN police monitors. There is a sentence that says: "The role of the United Nations police monitors would be to ensure that the local police forces carry out their duties without discriminating between different ethnic groups and without violating anybody's human rights." So UN police monitors were to ensure regular work by the police, not disarming or anything else. They were only to supervise how the police operate. That was in item 7, and maybe that was confused with a later explanation by Mr. Kostic as to how Croat armed forces tried to penetrate and to disarm the police in those areas.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That has been clarified. It was the way it came across in translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I take it that "local police forces," the phrase used in Article 7, would be difficult to define. There appear to have been official and unofficial police forces. So was there uncertainty about what "local police force" meant?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may explain. The Vance Plan envisaged only a truce and the engagement of peacekeepers to protect the Serb population in these areas. However, it did not prejudice or favour any political solution and did not favour any existing political situation in these territories. In other words, for the Serb people in Krajina, continued to have what they had before the peacekeepers came: Their police stations, their police force, their system of education, their Cyrillic alphabet, their judiciary; all the functions that they ran in the Krajinas, they kept after the peacekeepers came.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Kostic, in an area where the Serb population was a substantial minority, would there be a Serb police station and a Croatian police station, therefore two local police forces, or would there only be a Croatian police force?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There would have been no Serb or Croat police forces. The police forces that existed there at the moment peacekeepers came continued to be there, continued to exist. In areas where Serbs were a substantial minority and the police station was ran by Croats, nothing in that police station would have changed. But that was precisely the role of the monitors, police monitors mentioned in item 7 of the Vance Plan. They were to see to it that, regardless of whether the Serbs are a majority or minority in a certain area, the police forces in a particular station should treat all ethnicities equally and treat everyone equally.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: To save time, could you just read the last sentence in item 11, which begins: "Should there be serious tensions ..."

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Should there be serious tensions between ethnic groups within -- within -- between ethnic groups within a UNPA, the United Nations forces would place themselves between the two sides in order to prevent hostilities."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, would you please compare these tasks of the peacekeepers with the role of the JNA in the next paragraphs.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were completely the same. That's why we were pleased with the Vance Plan and the whole approach of Mr. Cyrus Vance and his associates relating to the drafting of this plan. The JNA had the task to stand between the conflicting parties in case a conflict arises and to prevent these tensions from turning into war.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, tell me about the mandate of the UNPROFOR. You said that the main role in bringing them was played by politicians from Montenegro and Serbia. How does the mandate of the UNPROFOR fit within the theory of territorial aspirations of Serbia against other countries?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It makes absolutely no sense, because this mandate of the UNPROFOR refutes the theory that there were any territorial ambitions of Serbia or anybody else against others.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Would it be fair to say that I wanted to keep these territories under my control and therefore I asked the UN peacekeepers to come?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot explain such a theory at all. It makes no sense. We were pulling out the JNA and bringing the blue helmets.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Look at paragraph 109 of the Croatian indictment. I won't be reading it whole, just the part that relates to the Vance Plan. It says: "Under the Vance Plan, four United Nations Protected Areas, UNPAs, were established in the areas occupied -" occupied mind you - "by Serb force forces. The Vance Plan called for the withdrawal of the JNA from Croatia and the return of displaced persons to their homes in the UNPAs. Although the JNA officially withdrew from Croatia in May 1992, large portions of its weaponry and personnel remained in the Serb-held areas and were turned over to the police of the Republic of Serbian Krajina, RSK. Displaced persons were not allowed to return to their homes and those few Croats and other non-Serbs who had remained in the Serb occupied areas were expelled in the following months. The territory of the RSK remained under Serb occupation until large portions of it were retaken by Croatian forces in two operations in 1995." What is written in this paragraph, does it correspond to what you know about it?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Practically nothing of what you read corresponds with what I know. Mr. Cyrus Vance and his team who defined the so-called Vance Plan, and Mr. Vance personally, he was an earnest, serious statement, a highly qualified diplomat, and he was characterised by great objectivity in analysing and resolving the problems that arose in these areas. We just explained the purpose of the Vance Plan. What is written in the indictment I can only interpret as an ill-intentioned phrase of the -- or a version of the OTP, because the JNA completely withdrew from those areas, and those areas were put under the control of the United Nations. So this language must be ill-intentioned on the part of the Prosecution. If the OTP had the least desire to objectively portray the situation, they would have at least looked at the language of the Vance Plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, compare these two sentences. In the indictment, it says: "Under the Vance Plan, four UNPAs were established in the areas occupied by Serb forces," whereas the Vance Plan says these would be "areas where Serbs constitute a majority or a substantial minority and where recent inter-ethnic tensions have turned into a crisis." How would you comment on this comparison?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is an obvious clash between the two versions, and I can only treat it as ill-intentioned.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honours, objection against this line of questioning. It's up to the Judges to actually decide what was -- what conclusion needs to be drawn from the fact -- from the facts. It's not for the witness to comment constantly on ill-intentions of the Prosecution and the like. I reject that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff. Perhaps you're a little bit too sensitive, though. I don't know whether it's -- it's not a comment that the witness can make. May I make this comment, however: Mr. Milosevic, you're putting to the witness that paragraph 109 does not coincide with the Vance Plan. The Vance Plan, I think, referred to areas under Serb occupation or where the Serbs were in a substantial minority.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: "... where the Serbs constituted a majority or a substantial minority ..." Why would you say that this is inconsistent as a summary of the phrase?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You can compare this for yourself. In the paragraph I quoted, it says that according to that plan, four zones or areas were established in the areas occupied by Serb forces. Mention is made of occupied areas, whereas the Vance Plan mentions areas in which the Serbs constitute a majority or a numerous minority and where there are tensions following from recent conflicts. There is a difference here, and I want to establish it with this witness, who was a direct participant in the drawing up and implementation of this plan.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. But I think Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff is correct, that the conclusions to be drawn as to the differences are matters that are best left for the Trial Chamber. Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: When did the JNA withdraw from the UN protected areas?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that the exact date is impossible to establish, because we had an enormous problem. The Croatian paramilitary formations and the Croatian leadership could not be brought to stop violating the cease-fire. We invested a lot of effort in contacts with Mr. Marrack Goulding and Mr. Cyrus Vance in order to start implementing the peace plan gradually and start bringing in the peacekeeping forces in those areas where peace had already been established, leaving for later those areas where the cease-fire was still being violated. On the 2nd of January, 1992, Mr. Cyrus Vance stated that the plan had been drawn up, and I know for sure that on the 9th of March in the Federation Palace in Belgrade, I received a numerous delegation, headed by the Indian general, Satish Nambiar, who was the first commander of the UN peacekeeping forces in the area of the Republic of Serbian Krajina. The units of the JNA finally and definitely withdrew from the whole territory in May 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And where were weapons kept in the Krajina, how were they guarded, and were they taken from the depots; and if so, when?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The demilitarisation of the area and the withdrawal of the JNA was the burning issue that the local population could not accept because they were afraid that the international forces would not be able to fulfil their role of protecting them, and in the end this proved to be so; they really weren't. The Vance Plan envisaged that members of the Territorial Defence originating from the territory of Serbian Krajina and the long barrels of the police forces, as well as all heavy weapons, should be kept in depots on the territory of the Republic of Serbian Krajina. They were to be kept under two keys. One would be held by representatives of the UN and the other by representatives of the Serb population of the area. If there was a physical threat to the Serb people in the areas protected by the UN, and only in such cases, could the weapons be taken from the depots. In one case this actually happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: After the UN forces arrived in these protected areas, who, according to your knowledge, violated the cease-fire and the UN Security Council Resolution?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, although I can talk only about the period until mid-June 1992, it was exclusively the paramilitary formations of Croatia that violated the cease-fires in the UN protected areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Lord Owen, in his book "Balkan Odyssey," which has been tendered into evidence here, on page 97 wrote the following: "In late 1992, the arms embargo hardly touched Croatia. Although the SRJ sent to the Security Council details on arms shipments, nothing was done to prevent them. Very soon the Croatian army armed itself with planes, heavy artillery, and other weapons, and most of these were bought in East Germany. This was happening before the eyes of the Serbs and, therefore, it was easy to understand why they resisted demilitarisation. The Croatian Serbs were a consolidating factor while the Croatian government was a destabilising factor." This is a quotation from Lord Owen's book. What do you know about this and was Lord Owen right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My knowledge is identical to what has been stated by Lord Owen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You must ask the witness a more specific question. That is an invitation for the professor to speak for five or ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The response took five seconds, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Has he answered? Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And does the following statement in the indictment correspond to what you know?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What statement are you referring to? What is "the following statement" to which you are referring?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not looking at the transcript, so I don't know what has been interpreted to you. I said, "Does the statement from the indictment correspond to what you know?"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What paragraph, then? What paragraph in the indictment are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The one I've already quoted. "The territory of the RSK remained under Serb occupation until 1995, when the Croatian forces --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's paragraph 109, the penultimate sentence in paragraph 109.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: "... when the Croatian forces in two operations retook large portions of that territory." My question is: Does this statement correspond to what you know? And before you answer, I will only read out to you a part of a testimony on page 28521 by Lord Owen here, who says -- that's 28521: "[In English] ... it does need to be remembered that one of the biggest ethnic cleansings in the whole of the Balkans during this period was that involving Serbs who had to flee Krajina in the early summer of 1995 and that, when we talk about this whole complex of problems, we have to recognise that one of the biggest failures was the failure to ensure that the ordinary citizens in Croatia who were Serbs were entitled -- were able to continue to live there." [Interpretation] How does this fit in, to the best of your knowledge and in view of what Lord Owen said, that the territory remained under Serb occupation until 1995, until large portions of it were retaken by Croatian forces in two operations in 1995?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said just a moment ago that the UN peacekeeping forces and the peacekeeping operation unfortunately failed to fulfil their purpose, which was to protect the Serb population until a political solution was found for the status of that population on those territories. Evidently there is a discrepancy between what is stated in this paragraph of the indictment and the observations and statements made by Lord Owen. From what the indictment says, one might simply conclude that the authors of the indictment were praising and rewarding those who perpetrated the crime and those who perpetrated the largest genocide after World War II until today by driving out vast numbers of Serb people from the territory of Croatia. In other words, they were attempting to reward the criminal and to transform the victim into a criminal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Impermissible comment. Impermissible comment that last one, Professor. Just answer the question and we'll get on much better. And you must refrain from comments like that. Confine yourself to the questions that are asked. You're not helping the cause of Mr. Milosevic in any way by these gratuitous comments.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But I'm not here to help Mr. Milosevic but to help you, to tell you the truth as a direct participant in these events, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You're not helping me. You're not helping the Chamber by those gratuitous comments. Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In his book, Lord Owen on page 61, in the first paragraph, he says: "They likewise resisted the Croatian state in other areas of Croatia, such as Slavonia, Baranja, and so on, which formed the military border of the Krajina under the Austrian-Habsburg rule. And this was felt especially strongly after 1945 where, after World War II, the inhabitants were exposed to genocide by the Croatian Ustasha. Very few commentators understood in 1995 that the Croatian government, by attacking the Krajina, was not liberating or retaking this territory as the Serbs had inhabited it for over three centuries." My question to you is: From your own standpoint and according to what Lord Owen states here, in this paragraph of the indictment I have quoted to you, could it be said that the territory of the RSK remained under Serb occupation until 1995?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: By no means. This territory could not have been occupied by a population that had resided there for several hundred years. The units of the JNA, even if the Prosecution were to call them Serb units, had withdrawn completely from those territories. The territories were demilitarised. It was the Serb population that had resided there for hundreds of years that remained, as well as the blue helmets of the UN, battalions from many countries. So one really cannot speak of Serb occupation of those territories. However, I will refrain from commenting or drawing any conclusions after Mr. Robinson's warning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What Lord Owen calls one of the largest ethnic cleansing operations is viewed as an occupation to liberate or retake occupied territory in the indictment, and what Lord Owen says was the ethnic cleansing of the territory, these people are called occupiers in the indictment. Which of these is true?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already answered that question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, he has already answered that. Let's move on to another question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Professor Kostic, do you know the efforts made by part of the leadership of Krajina, led by Milan Babic, to proclaim Krajina as being joined to Serbia?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Babic not only attempted to impose on the Serb leadership a decision to conjoin the Republic of Serbian Krajina to Serbia, but Mr. Babic also tried to impose this on the Presidency of the SFRY, that is to say that their Presidencies -- their members should become members of the SFRY, which we refused to do. And after that, we were proclaimed traitors, the traitors of the interests of the Serbian people. I mean -- when I say "us," I mean us, members of the Presidency.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What about the authorities in Serbia? What was their reaction to that?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I know that the Assembly of Serbia, in that regard, adopted -- I think it was a declaration. I'm not quite sure, but I think it was a declaration where the Assembly of Serbia put up reservations towards this demand made by the leadership of Serb Krajina and Mr. Babic. They refused to accept it and just strove to find a peaceful settlement for the status of the nation in Croatia. And I can say that with regard to the formation of the Republic of Serb Krajina, as vice-president of the Yugoslav state Presidency, I read about that in the papers. That's how I came to learn of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: When you read that news, were you able to assess and do you know what the immediate reason was or pretext was for the formation of the Republic of Serbian Krajina?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The immediate reason to bring in a decision to form Serbian Krajina on the 19th of December, 1991, was something that took place two days earlier, that is to say a resolution or declaration made by the European Community, that is to say on the 17th of December, 1991. There were, I think, two declarations; one relating to the criteria for recognition of countries and states as independent states, and the second resolution was the resolution on Yugoslavia by which the Yugoslav federal republics were called upon by the 23rd of December, 1991, to table a request for recognising their independence. And that resolution on the part of the European Community was the -- was final and definitive, and it meant leaving behind the concept that the Yugoslav -- that the European Community had advocated thus far. That concept was left behind overnight when it wanted to find a political solution to the Yugoslav crisis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, in that regard, the reactions to this in Serbia and the reactions of its parliament, was there anything there that could have the sound of territorial pretensions or that could resemble any territorial pretensions on the part of Serbia covering territories outside its republic?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, certainly not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: We have here in tab 71 the declaration of the Assembly of Serbia, in which it says under III: "That is why the Republic of Serbia will strive for peace and a political settlement to the crisis in Yugoslavia which should enable the affirmation of democratic methods for overcoming the crisis and equal respect of the legitimate interests of all the Yugoslav peoples and republics. "In that sense, the Republic of Serbia firmly supports the efforts of the United Nations towards an urgent cessation of the military conflicts, the establishment of a stable peace, and the creation of the conditions necessary for continuation of the political negotiation process under the competence and authority of the world organisation, all-encompassing solution to the Yugoslav state crisis in a just and lasting manner." So that's what it says there. These positions, do they coincide and are they the same as the assumptions that actually Serbia was endeavouring to strengthen its power and authority over that part of the country at all and realise any of its territorial pretensions?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that statements of that kind are completely fabricated, and I confirmed a moment ago what you read out in point III of the declaration of the Serb Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, just a couple of questions related to the fact that in this indictment mention is made of Dubrovnik. What do you know about the events in and around Dubrovnik? What can you tell us?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, on one of the previous days I already said that neither Dubrovnik nor Vukovar happened just by chance, that Tudjman had attempted in every way possible to have the flames of war burn in other parts of the country; and Dubrovnik is bordering on Montenegro, Vukovar borders on Serbia. And many people asked me in the bygone period who took the decision and how this came about, how the Dubrovnik operation came about in the first place. And on every occasion I had just one answer to give to that question: There was no decision by the Yugoslav state Presidency in that sense, nor would the Presidency ever be in a position to take a decision of that kind. The deployment of the units of the Yugoslav People's Army over a territory which was defined by the constitution as part of Yugoslavia, and the deployment of those units which, pursuant to the Yugoslav constitution, were duty-bound to preserve the territorial integrity and system of the country, the only person in authority to deploy these units was the General Staff or, rather, in a situation where there was an imminent threat of war, it was the staff of the Supreme Command, regardless of the fact that Dubrovnik was very much abused by the media when an attack on the Yugoslav army took place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'm going to stop you and ask Mr. Milosevic to put a specific question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What was the reason for a conflict to break out there, around Dubrovnik, those surroundings?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we on the territory of Dubrovnik had not had a single armed soldier for 20 years, a single armed JNA soldier. Only on the Prevlaka peninsula, which is the border, the very border with Montenegro - it is a sharp peninsula at the entrance to the Bay of Kotor, which is where there was a barracks or, rather, a military training centre for marksmanship. And despite the fact that for a full 20 years we had not a single JNA soldier, armed soldier on the territory of Dubrovnik, in that period suddenly the number of armed police units on the Croatian side increased a great deal, and it was these training grounds and the barracks there at Prevlaka, at the Prevlaka peninsula, that the armed provocations and attacks started. And that, in fact, was the basic reason for which the staff of the Supreme Command, to the best of my knowledge and information, sent units of the Yugoslav People's Army to the territory. And I personally think that the Supreme Command Staff acted correctly in doing so and that it was thanks to their intervention that the war was stopped from spreading from Croatia to the territory of the other republics.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, ask me -- please tell me, did Serbia have anything to do with the events in the Dubrovnik region, any of them, any of the ones mentioned here?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, nothing whatsoever to do with that. I explained the deployment of the units and that it was the Supreme Command Staff who were in charge of deploying them. And as far as I know, the leadership of Serbia had no competence or influence for a similar operation that took place in Vukovar, although it is at the borders of Serbia, between Croatia and Serbia, Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Professor Kostic, do you know that in this alleged Croatian indictment and Bosnian indictment are named, together with me and other individuals, as a participant of this alleged joint criminal enterprise?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you some questions now first relating to the Croatian part of the indictment. In paragraph 7, for instance, of the Croatian indictment, at the time when this joint criminal enterprise came into existence and continued, it says the following: "This joint criminal enterprise came into existence before the 1st of August, 1991, and continued until at least June 1992." Where were you and what were you doing during that period of time? That is before the 1st of August, 1991, until at least June 1992.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Throughout that time, I was vice-president of the Yugoslav state Presidency.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And what was your function as vice-president of the Yugoslav state Presidency, and what was its relationship or what did it have to do with the events and conduct of the Yugoslav People's Army at that time?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The operative leadership of the Yugoslav People's Army was performed by the professional organ, that is to stay the staff of the Supreme Command. They were in charge of that. The SFRY Presidency as the Supreme Command, as a body and the highest civilian control of the Yugoslav People's Army, had, pursuant to the constitution, its functions and role, and that was that through its decisions it should create conditions for the JNA for it to be able to perform its role to protect the constitutional order and territorial integrity of the country. And in that sense, the SFRY Presidency did have under its competence and authority to make decisions, for example, about raising combat readiness in cases when the JNA barracks, for example, which were under siege, which were blocked and directly attacked, you didn't need a separate decision there because the army had to act in self-defence when it was under a blockade. But we could raise combat readiness for the army and bring in reinforcements, proclaim mobilisation, which was very topical at that time, because both the Slovenes and the Croats and also the Albanians and later on the Muslims in Bosnia ceased to send in their recruits to the Yugoslav People's Army. And then additional mobilisation had to be resorted to to bring the army up to full strength, to ensure that it was capable of protecting the part of the population that expressed the desire to continue living together in the state which was Yugoslavia. And if we were to quote the most important decisions taken by the Presidency itself, for example --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, next question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, Professor Kostic, you described your authorisations and competencies, as well as that of the Presidency, as the Supreme Commander of the JNA. Would you please now answer this question: Did I -- and here we have this date the 1st of August and I asked you what you did until June 1992. Now, what about me? Did I have any competence and authority at that time over the JNA?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, you were the President of Serbia, throughout that period of time, and as such you had no competence and authority over the Yugoslav People's Army. That is quite certain. And in the indictment, in several portions of the indictment, it mentions that you established complete control over the Presidency as the Supreme Command, which is also incorrect. And if I want to tell the truth to the very end, to tell the whole truth, I cannot say or claim how much or to what extent Mr. Jovic, for example, who was a member of the Presidency himself, from Serbia - yes, from Serbia - to what extent he communicated with you. But I can say for certain that you didn't have any control over me. There are many elements on which I can say that and evidence which bears that out, bears that conclusion of mine out, and ultimately Mr. Jovic and I did not agree on many issues. But where we did agree, Mr. Jovic and you and I myself and the other members of the Presidency, was the basic idea that we had advocated from the very beginning; that was to preserve our communality, to preserve Yugoslavia as far as we were able, and to protect the interests of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Professor, when you say that as the President of Serbia Mr. Milosevic had no competence nor authority over the Yugoslav People's Army, do you have in mind legal constitutional authority as distinct from de facto authority?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Legally de facto he had no authority, could not have had any authority. That is incontestable. Except from the 27th of April, 1992, when the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia was constituted. At that time the Presidency, until the first president, Mr. Cosic, was elected, it performed the function of president of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, Mr. Milosevic, from the 27th of April, 1992, and Mr. Bulatovic, as president of Montenegro, represented the Supreme Defence Council pursuant to the new constitution of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. But up until then, in formal terms and in legal terms, Mr. Milosevic had no authority or competence. Whether de facto he did have any, in practice, that is, I can say he did in practice as much as he had political authority, and he had quite a lot of political authority, political standing. And as you were able to notice, not only did he have political authority and the force of that political authority in Yugoslavia and in Serbia and in Montenegro and in many areas, but he enjoyed that political authority also vis-a-vis many international factors, factors of the -- in the international community, which, when they concluded agreements with the SFRY Presidency or, rather, with Mr. Kadijevic and with Mr. Tudjman as with two parties, two sides who were in conflict, they insisted that Mr. Milosevic appear on the scene, although there were no legal -- there was no legal authorisation. But thanks to his political authority and political influence, they thought he could contribute to quelling the situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In view of the fact that you were the head of the Presidency, which was the Supreme Command as a body, do you know of any single intervention on my part where I de facto would have exerted any influence towards the JNA?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only one detail, which I noted in my book which is to be found in tab 73. When it came to the Yugoslav People's Army, when you directly contacted me, there's just one detail there, and that was in the afternoon when you rang me up on the phone one day and expressed your dissatisfaction because General Marko Negovanovic had been retired who at that point in time was pensioned. The minister -- he was the minister of defence of Serbia, but he wasn't pensioned as a minister of defence of Serbia but as a general, who during the time of the Slovenian operation, was at the head of the 12th KOS administration, and his deputy was Aleksandar Vasiljevic. So that operation we assessed as being very wrong, that operation in Slovenia. And I personally considered that if Mr. Veljko Kadijevic or General Adzic could have made a mistake in their assessments to the effect that the Territorial Defence of Slovenia would turn their weapons against the JNA, I considered that that could not have happened to Mr. Marko Negovanovic and Mr. Aco Vasiljevic. Now, your intervention followed and came about because that person was retired, was pensioned off without my having informed you, and it was my duty to inform you because you were the president of Serbia and he was the minister of defence of Serbia, that is to say in your own republic. I tried to inform you before you actually rang me up. I left a message with your chef de cabinet, which I don't suppose reached you, and that was the only intervention on your part that I had from you for one year. Of course, I explained to you on that occasion that we hadn't pensioned off Mr. Negovanovic as defence minister but as the previous head of the 12th administration, KOS administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Now, my protest, was it the -- was I protesting because I said that was what should have been done, that you should have informed me if you pensioned off somebody, or because of the reasons for that being done?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I said that I understood your reaction, and I expected a reaction from you, in fact, and that is why I wanted to inform you of it before you read about it in the newspapers, precisely because we were dealing with the minister of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did my reaction have anything to do with your decision to pension him off?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I will just remind everybody, if the Trial Chamber allows me: Concerning the Slovenia operation, Mr. Veljko Kadijevic made a press release, a communique where he admitted publicly that the General Staff had made an error of judgement, and he publicly confessed to it. And in the Assembly of Montenegro that elected me while this Slovene crisis was still going on and the MPs had raised the question of responsibility for this Slovenia adventure, as they called it, I said that the priority was to establish a truce on the Slovene border.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... question. I think we have dealt with this single aberration sufficiently.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Please, Professor Kostic, tell us very briefly, what was your relationship with others mentioned in paragraph 7 as participants in the joint criminal enterprise: Milosevic, Jovic, Branko Kostic - that's you - Kadijevic, Adzic, Babic, Martic, Hadzic, Stanisic, Simatovic, Simovic, Seselj, Bulatovic, Vasiljevic, Stojicic, Raznjatovic? What kind of relationship did you have with these people? Was there a common denominator among those listed in paragraph 7?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Among all those names you mentioned, it is very difficult to find even one common denominator that could have linked us all. Some of those people I have never met or known. Another number I split up with very soon, either because they were pensioned off or their term of service expired, such as Mr. Kadijevic, who already on the 8th of January --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You don't have to go into specifics. That will take up a lot of time.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But I never met, for instance, Mr. Zeljko Raznjatovic. Mr. Seselj I met only once, when I was addressing a gathering of Serb refugees from Western Slavonia, and another time before the election of the first president of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia; never again. I've never met Mr. Frenki Simatovic. Who else is mentioned? Badza, I've never met him either. As for you, Mr. Milosevic, I met you for the first time when I took the office of president of Presidency of Montenegro. Mr. Bulatovic I had not known from before until in 1989 we found ourselves in the Montenegrin leadership together. Mr. Jovic I remembered from working in the industry. He was later a minister, a cabinet minister, and later ambassador to Rome. The other two members of the Presidency I had not met before either. And as for General Kadijevic, General Adzic, and Stane Brovet, I met them for the first time when I became vice-president of the SFRY Presidency. There was a very brief time, and before that I didn't really know them. And the same goes for many other military leaders. For instance, General Simovic and Mr. Kovsek, who was one of corps commanders, I met in Podgorica while they were there. But as for the other elements - political, ideological and every other - this is a very varied crowd, so to speak, and they don't have anything in common.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You said several times about something that linked together those members of the Presidency who remained in their office in the Presidency. It was their commitment to preserving Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Was that commitment the obligation for both me, Kostic, Bajramovic, and all the others who stayed on the Presidency?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It resulted from our personal conviction, I would say, but it was also our constitutional obligation indubitably, whereas the others violated their obligation and committed an act of treason.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How do you explain this now? We had the constitutional obligation to do everything in our power to preserve Yugoslavia, which was the only internationally recognised legitimate entity. This commitment of ours to preserve Yugoslavia, which is defined here as a joint criminal enterprise, is opposed to violent and unilateral secession that was even overturned by the Constitutional Court, is qualified as a democratic act. How can you explain that? What possible reasoning could be behind it?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really have no explanation for this. I tried, while I read the indictment, where my name is mentioned in several places, I really tried hard to find some sort of connection, some way in which this conclusion would be possible, but I did not succeed. And throughout the indictment it is alleged that you had control over that Presidency, especially over Jovic and me, and there are constant references to the joint criminal enterprise, and I kept expecting to find somewhere in that indictment those criminal decisions taken by that Presidency, either under your control or outside of it, but regrettably, I didn't find any such thing. "Regrettably" is perhaps not the best term. I didn't find, even in the indictment, any criminal decisions taken by the Presidency. I am glad, and I'm proud of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did the Presidency take a single decision to inflame the conflicts, to commit any aggressive act or violate anybody's right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No such decision was taken, either by the complete or by the reduced Presidency, to use the term used by Mr. Robinson, which is completely adequate; "reduced" rather than "Rump" Presidency. And our greatest commitment concerning the JNA were the 14 cease-fires that Mr. Kadijevic constantly kept concluding on our behalf, with our approval, on our instructions. And if there were certain misunderstandings in the course of those negotiations, Mr. Kadijevic always expressed his reservation and said that he had to consult the Presidency of the SFRY. Let me remind you, one of those negotiations --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You were asked whether the Presidency took any decision to inflame the conflict or to commit any aggressive act or violate anybody's right. I'd like to reformulate it and ask you whether the Presidency took any decision that had the effect, that could be said to have had the effect of inflaming the conflict. You see the difference?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I'm trying. I'm trying to understand the distinction, but even when you reformulate the question like that, I cannot see a single decision taken by the Presidency that could have inflamed the conflict.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. It's time to adjourn. We will take the break for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Professor Kostic, I'll read to you a bit of the transcript from the questioning of witness -- Prosecution witness General Vasiljevic that relates to the issue of his influence on army leadership. "Question: Since we have established that I could not have influence over the military leadership like General Kadijevic, [In English] for instance. "Answer: I don't think you could have. "And General Kadijevic was in his position until January 1992? "Yes. Until the 8th of January, 1992. "So was there any possibility for anyone from Serbia and I personally to influence the changes that had taken place up until then? Any kind of personnel changes in the army. "Until the end of 1991, there was no possibility." [Interpretation] I'll skip over a bit. "[In English] And when Kadijevic explained that he was getting on and that his health was not at its best, do you remember the explanation that he gave for leaving the position of Federal Secretary and that he was succeeded by Blagoje Adzic? "Yes. "Blagoje Adzic, had he been in any way the number two man in the military leadership? "Yes. "Did anyone influence the appointment of Adzic? "There was some influence over him when he retired. "And when did Adzic retire? "After the 8th of May, 1992."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Time for a question now, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honours, can we please have the reference number from the transcript, because Mr. Milosevic didn't give it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic. Please give the transcript page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Electronic page is 16227.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You have been assisted by Judge Kwon. He says it's 16227.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: 17th of February.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Please ask a question now, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So, this was the testimony of General Vasiljevic relating to my possible influence over the military leadership up to May 1992. What do you know about that? Does that coincide with what you know or not? Did I have any influence over the military leadership, at least until that particular date?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In view of the shortness of the period I was on the Presidency of the SFRY, I personally think that General Vasiljevic was in a much better position to make that estimate, but what he said does coincide with what I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I will now ask you about the pensioning off that occurred while you were vice-president of the Presidency. The transcript goes on to say: "[In English] Can we then state that on the basis of what you are testifying about, until the 8th of May when Blagoje Adzic retired, there was no theoretical possibility for someone from Serbia, and I personally -- personally to influence the army, the JNA? Is that right or not? "That is not right. I've already said, I don't know whether it was in private session or public session, but never mind, I can say this in public session as well, I mentioned the example of the retirement of 33 generals in February 1992 when General Blagoje Adzic addressed you in connection with the reasons for the retirement of my deputy. So he didn't address himself to Branko Kostic who signed the decrees but he addressed you." [Interpretation] Now, would you please explain, Professor Kostic, how did it happen that 33 generals were pensioned off, and did I have any involvement in it?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me say first that when we made the decision to pension off 33 generals, I as vice-president of the Presidency asked Mr. Adzic to bring me the next day the appropriate decrees to sign. However, Mr. Adzic replied that he needed five days to do that, and I accepted his answer. Over those five days, there were many interventions by Mr. Jovic concerning a few of the generals, and the number was reduced from 33 to 28. And then in that first round, 28 generals were pensioned off.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Just a moment. You said Mr. Jovic intervened, not I. Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, that's missing from the transcript, Mr. Robinson: Not I.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, we take note of that, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I continue? The greatest number of those generals who were pensioned off, and all of them were honourable, honest people who had on one or another ground envisaged by the law been entitled to retirement. By that time the army had only half its personnel, and the Territorial Defence too. So the pensioning off of this first group was not an unusual move on the part of the Presidency or me or anybody. We were reducing the number of generals through the system of retirement, because even if Yugoslavia had remained in its previous size, we did have a surplus, an exaggerated number of generals in the Yugoslav People's Army. Why did Mr. Jovic exert that pressure? I really never discussed it with him, but I thought, and I still think, that he had been in Belgrade in prominent positions for a long time. He had been on the Presidency for two or three years, either as a member or vice-president or even president. He knew all those people among the generals much better, and it is not impossible that he was intervening as a friend, as a human being, because he had been asked by some of those generals to not pension them off. So we reduced this number from 33 to 28. And concerning one of the generals, who was the deputy and the one mentioned by Aleksandar Vasiljevic, that's Mr. Tumanov, he was Aleksandar Vasiljevic's deputy in the 12th administration of the counter-intelligence service, KOS. I insisted, and the Presidency accepted, not to pension off Mr. Tumanov but to move him from the position of deputy head of the 12th administration of KOS because we had certain information that, as an ethnic Macedonian, he had displayed an interest in Macedonian senior officers. In fact, he inquired with them whether they would be willing to move to Macedonian units.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Professor Kostic, you did not answer the second part of my question: Did I have anything at all to do with the pensioning off of those generals? Did I influence their pensioning off at all, or did I intervene not to pension someone off?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Never on any occasion, including this one, did you call me or exert any influence at all. I cannot say whether or not you communicated with Jovic about this. I can neither confirm or deny that, but I'm sure that you had no influence. And the best evidence for that, to show that you had no influence at all about this, is the example of the pensioning off of the second group of generals, which took place in May. You practically didn't even know that your minister of defence, General Negovanovic, was on this list of generals to be pensioned off.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In paragraph 6 of the Croatia indictment, it says: "The purpose of this joint criminal enterprise was the forcible removal of the majority of the Croat and other non-Serb population from the approximately one-third of the territory of the Republic of Croatia that he -" and this refers to me - "planned to become part of a new Serb-dominated state through the commission of crimes in violation of articles ..." and it doesn't matter which ones. "These areas included those regions that were referred to by Serb authorities and are hereinafter referred to as the 'Serbian Autonomous District Krajina,' 'Western Slavonia,' and 'Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem,' and the 'Dubrovnik Republic.'" As your name is mentioned in connection with this enterprise, tell me quite specifically: Did a joint criminal enterprise exist? In particular, there was any plan or goal of forcibly removing the Croatian or other non-Serb population from one-third of the territory of the Republic of Croatia which I allegedly planned to become a Serb-dominated area through the commission of crimes?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Professor, concentrate on the issue of fact, not the question of law as to the existence of a joint criminal enterprise. Yes, please answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I can only speak about the facts, then I can only say that this is a purely fabricated claim in the indictment, and the Prosecution would have to explain to you as the Trial Chamber how such nonsense can be alleged, because it is well known --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Professor, you were specifically asked questions that relate to the fact. Was there any plan or goal of forcibly removing the Croatian or other non-Serb population from one-third of the territory of the Republic of Croatia? What's your answer to that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Such a plan did not exist. Can I add a sentence, please, Mr. Robinson?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Official information, which can be found on the internet, indicates that the ethnic make-up of the population of Croatia from 1991 to 2001, in view of the participation of Croats in the overall breakdown has been increased from 79. These are specific facts. Croatia. From 77.9 per cent, the ethnic Croatian population in the overall population of Croatia in 2001 amounted to 89.63 per cent. In other words, the part of Croats has been increased by over 11 per cent in the intervening years. In the same period of time, the overall population of Croatia, in 2001, had 12.2 per cent of Serbs, in the overall Croatian population. This was in 1991. And in 2001 - and this is official information that can be found on the internet concerning the census in Croatia - ten years later the Serbs in Croatia were reduced to 4.5 per cent. I think these are specific facts --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- which no Prosecutor can deny.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Paragraph 26 of the Croatia indictment, the methods by which this alleged joint criminal enterprise were implemented are listed. It says: "Slobodan Milosevic, acting alone and in concert with other members of the joint criminal enterprise -" that's you and others - "participated in the joint criminal enterprise in the following ways: "(a) provided direction and assistance to the political leadership of the SAO SBWS, the SAO Western Slavonia, the SAO Krajina and RSK on the takeover of these areas and the subsequent forcible removal of the Croat and other non-Serb population." My question to you is the following: The takeover of these areas, who was in power in those areas?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The representatives of the Serbian people, such as Babic, Martic, Dokmanovic, Veselinovic, and so on. So this allegation is incorrect. There was no takeover of power because it was the representatives of the Serbian people who had had power before.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did I or you or others in Belgrade ever see or meet these people before they became people holding power in those areas?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For myself, I can assert that I never saw those people before that and that I only met them for the first time as a member of the state commission to which I was appointed as chairman to go to Knin. Tupurkovski and Bogicevic went to see Tudjman in Zagreb. This was done with a view to securing respect for the cease-fire. I cannot say whether you had met them previously or not, but I can say that communication with those people began when those people had already established their organs of government on those territories of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Could anyone have taken over power when they were already in power?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already answered that question: They were already in power, so they didn't have to take it over.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: When the HDZ came into power in Croatia, did they forcibly try to take power from those Serbs in areas where Serbs were in the majority?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've answered that. They sent special units, police units to take over police stations in those Serb territories, to disarm those policemen who were representatives of the local Serb population, and that's what led to the conflicts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did the constitutions of the SFRY and the republics of the SFRY permit associations of municipalities?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Could they do this on their own initiative or did they need approval for that?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It could be done on the initiative of the municipalities themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And those entities mentioned under 26(a): The SAO, SBWS, the SAO Western Slavonia, the SAO Krajina and so on, how were these formed?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will tell you another undisputable fact which could be of interest to the Trial Chamber and which will challenge everything that is said in this indictment about an alleged plan for a joint criminal enterprise, and this information is as follows: A community of municipalities, or an association of municipalities, in areas where there was a majority Serb population in Croatia occurred after the adoption of the constitution in which the Serb people were thrown out as a constituent people and reduced to the status of an ethnic minority. This was a response of the Serbian population to the adoption of such a new constitution in Croatia. That's one element which cannot be disputed. Another one is the following: The formation of Serb autonomous provinces on Croatian territory occurred, if I'm correct, on the 28th of February, 1991. On the 18th or 22nd of February - I'm not sure exactly, but eight days before that - the Croatian government, already constituted by the HDZ after the elections, proposed to the Croatian parliament a constitutional law by which the Croatian parliament would declare that it would no longer respect the constitution of Yugoslavia or Yugoslav federal laws. So it was the actions of the Croatian government and parliament that occurred first. The formation of the Serb autonomous provinces was done in such a way that they had not yet seceded from Croatia. However, they stated that they would respect the constitution and laws of Yugoslavia.
