And thirdly, and very importantly, the Serbian Krajina was formed again as a response to moves by the Croatian government and the European Community. The Republic of Serbian Krajina was formed on the 19th of December, 1991, and two days previously the European Community had called on all Yugoslav republics to submit their applications for the recognition of independence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's a sufficient answer. Next question, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did the leaderships mentioned in the paragraph I have quoted from the indictment forcibly remove the Croat and other non-Serb population, and did they do this in connection with Serbia and with me?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, there was no previously planned forcible removal of the Croat and other non-Serb population. Everybody knows what happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Just a moment. I can hear you from a distance, but channel 6 is -- suddenly it's been cut off. There's no voice, no sound.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: May I ask the technical staff to look into that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Now suddenly it's back, although there's screeching. Got it now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I asked you whether the leaderships mentioned here forcibly removed the Croat and other non-Serb population.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't assert with certainty that there were no individual incidents and that there was no such behaviour by individuals in those leaderships. What I can assert is that there was no premeditated plan about the forcible removal of the Croat and other non-Serb population from that area. I can also assert with confidence that the JNA never resorted to such a measure, and I can reiterate what is common knowledge: On those territories where there were armed clashes due to the mounting inter-ethnic tensions, both the Serb and the Croat population from those areas attempted to flee and take refuge in areas where they would feel physically safer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In the Presidency of the SFRY, did you offer any assistance to the Krajina Serbs and their political leadership?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We as the Presidency did not have any special economic power. We felt the best assistance we could give them was by remaining consistent in our standpoint as the Supreme Command, to keep the JNA in those areas to provide physical protection to the population until a political solution of their status was found. I personally received two delegations from the leadership of the Serbian region of Western Slavonia, and there are minutes of this meeting. The Prosecution must have them, because it's been much easier for them than it has been for me to get hold of these minutes and other documents and all those records. In my two meetings with them, they expressed their great fear of what was to happen to them and asked us to deploy units of the JNA there. I told them that we were physically unable to do this because we did not have sufficient manpower. I therefore advised them not to raise tensions in those areas and that that would be their best protection. Unfortunately, the population of Western Slavonia experienced a large-scale exodus purely because we were unable to protect them with units of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And how did Serbia assist the Krajina Serbs?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In view of the fact there was discontinuity in communication, the Croats separated, the Croatian leadership separated from the Yugoslav constitutional laws, set themselves apart. And the Serb leadership on territories in Croatia no longer abided by Croatian laws and stated that they were going to respect the federal laws and federal constitution, and this gave rise to quite considerable problems in many areas; in food, supplies, and so on and so forth. So basic assistance to that population over there on the basis of their requests by their legitimate representatives had the character of humanitarian aid.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Do you have a date for when that happened, Professor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What are you referring to? A date for what?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: "The Serb leadership on territories in Croatia no longer abided by Croatian laws and stated that they were going to respect the federal laws and federal constitution, and that gave rise to considerable problems ..."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I've already said that the Croatian parliament enacted a constitution and its laws on the 20th of February, I think, give or take a day, 1991. And on the 28th of February, 1991, the leadership of the Serbian Autonomous Region passed a resolution stating that it would not be abiding by those Croatian laws but would be abiding by the Yugoslav constitution and federal laws. So it was from the end of February, roughly speaking, 1991 that the difficulties began arising in supplies coming in to the population, interruptions in communication and roads. Sometimes this was caused by the Serbian population themselves who wished to prevent the penetration of Croatian police to the areas to disarm police stations on their territory, but there's no specific date. You can't pinpoint it and say this started on such-and-such a date. But in many of the Serbian Krajinas the -- this period was different. But the communication lines and so on, they were most prominent in Western Slavonia, for example. But before these obstructions took place was in the Knin-Krajina area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In that same paragraph, 26(b), it says: "provided financial, material and logistical support for the regular and irregular military forces necessary for the takeover of these areas and the subsequent forcible removal of the Croat and other non-Serb population." Tell us, please, what were the regular or armed forces generally in that area, for example?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time in those areas, the only regular constitutionally founded and federal law founded existing armed forces were the forces of the Yugoslav People's Army, who were located there in peacetime as well, and the forces of the Territorial Defence, because in a situation with an imminent threat of war, all the armed formations, including the police and the police units and the volunteer units and the regular units of the JNA, all of them represented a united armed force under a united command, the command of the Supreme Command, the staff of the Supreme Command of the army of Yugoslavia and the General Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And who were the irregular forces then?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The irregular forces were all those forces which the Croatian leadership had established in the meantime, had armed in the meantime with weapons secretly coming into the country. I considered at the time - and still consider - that the irregular forces were the police forces that had multiplied in numbers, and I've already mentioned that, that in the space of two months alone the police forces burgeoned from 17.000 in peacetime in Croatia to 90.000 strong. And then there was the Croatian National Guards Corps, the armed citizens, depending on their political affiliation to the HDZ, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What about the Krajina Serbs? Were they the ones who were attacked or were they the ones who attacked?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, from what I've just said and from what I've been saying up to now, it is very clear that the Krajina Serbs didn't go and attack anybody anywhere. They were attacked and they were continuously attacked and everything they did they did to defend themselves and protect themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: A moment ago you explained the Croatian parliament bringing in a decision not recognising the Yugoslav constitution. Several days later they decided to adhere and abide by the Yugoslav constitution. Now their efforts along those lines, were they justified? Were they legal and lawful and considered as such, or not?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, bearing in mind the fact that Yugoslavia existed as the sole internationally recognised state and United Nations member until the 27th of April, 1992, and that all this was happening in 1991 and the bulk of it in the first half of 1991, it is quite clear that the strivings of the Krajina Serbs and the leadership of the Krajina Serbs was legitimate, legal, and based on the Yugoslav constitution.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In subparagraph (c) of paragraph 26, it says: "directed organs of the government of the Republic of Serbia to create armed forces separate from the federal armed forces to engage in combat activities outside the Republic of Serbia, particularly in the said areas in Croatia and the subsequent forcible removal of the Croat and other non-Serb population." Tell us now, please, did the Republic of Serbia ever form armed forces that were separate from the federal armed forces?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Under conditions in which the Yugoslav state existed, was there ever a plan to form any armed forces that would be separate from the federal armed forces?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Are you familiar with Article 132 of the constitution of Serbia, because it was -- this was the subject of many interpretations, erroneous ones and otherwise. What can you tell us about that article?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that article very well. I'm very familiar with it because it was indeed very often criticised and challenged and attacked by the secessionist republics. That particular article of the constitution of Serbia provided for the possibility that should it happen that the secessionist republics, bypassing the will and agreement of Serbia and other federal units which wished to remain together in a joint community within the state, so if those republics were to take secessionist steps, the constitution of Serbia provided through that article the fact that in cases of that kind the constitutional possibility is left open for Serbia to regulate questions which had hitherto come under the competence of the constitution of the SFRY.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But while the SFRY was in existence, did it precisely define that all questions coming under the competencies of the SFRY stay in those competencies?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. While the SFRY existed and the constitution of the SFRY existed and we expressed a maximum support and adherence to that constitution until it was revoked in 1992, the provisions of the federal constitution and federal laws governing that subject matter must be applied in the territory of Serbia as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In subparagraph (d), it says: "participated in the formation, financing, supply, support --" and so on and so forth -- "and direction of special forces of the Republic of Serbia Ministry of Internal Affairs. These special forces were created and supported to assist in the execution of the purpose of the joint criminal enterprise ..." Now, tell me, please, do you know whether the special forces of the MUP of Serbia or any other forces of the MUP of Serbia took part in anything that could be considered the execution on commission of some joint criminal enterprise or any crime whatsoever?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I really don't know anything that would indicate that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Now, had something like that existed, would you had have to have known about it, you and the other members of the SFRY Presidency?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it would have been quite natural that we were informed about things like that had they existed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In subparagraph (e) of paragraph 26, it says: "participated in providing financial, logistical and political support and direction to Serbian irregular forces and paramilitaries. Such support was given in furtherance of the joint criminal enterprise through ..." et cetera, et cetera. Now, please, do you know what the relationship between what -- the relationship between the leadership of Serbia, my own relationship to paramilitaries and your relationship and in the Presidency to paramilitaries?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know about that very well. I know what your attitude to them was like and I know what the attitude of the entire Serbian leadership in power in Serbia at the time was like as well as the Presidency, its attitude too towards these paramilitaries, paramilitary units that were established by different political parties: It was extremely negative. After working under conditions of an imminent threat of war, the law provided for the participation of volunteers, and that was regulated on the basis of the law. And as the Presidency and as the General Staff or the Supreme Command may -- issued specific orders, instructions, and guidelines, and so on. But when it came to paramilitaries, our -- our attitude was negative, and those paramilitaries at the time were established, as far as I know, by Vuk Draskovic, for instance, or his Serbian Revival Movement, which was an opposition party. Then there was Mirko Jovic, another case in point. Once again, a political party, an opposition political party at the time. So as far as I know, it was only Mr. Seselj and his radicals who organised volunteers from the ranks of his own party and his sympathisers. But as far as I know, there was not a single unit which acted as a unit of the radicals or as Seselj's unit. Those volunteers were sent to the competent commands of the Yugoslav People's Army or Territorial Defence, and they would then incorporate them and deploy them as the need arose into smaller units. And as far as I know, there was never any large unit or significant unit made up of, say, Seselj's volunteers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What was the JNA's attitude toward the paramilitaries?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The same as the Presidency of the SFRY and as was your attitude and the attitude in general of the Serbian authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You've already told us who formed paramilitaries in Serbia. Did the powers that be have anything to do with the formation of those paramilitaries?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. And I even think, if I might be allowed to express this view, that many opposition parties at that time, when the political fate and destiny both of the state and the people was decided, in those very dramatic and most dramatic times, a large number of opposition parties in Serbia found it more important to get rid of you, get you off the power structure and to set up their own power structures. So they thought that perhaps these paramilitaries coming back from the front could perhaps at one point in time be involved in that project that I mentioned a moment ago. And of course many times, through -- speaking at public meetings, I would issue warnings about the disagreement that existed among the Serb people and that they paid for dearly in this latest war.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Professor Kostic, we've seen that the local authorities, which later became the Serb autonomous regions, had even beforehand been in the hands of the representatives of the peoples that was the majority people in that area, which was the Serbs, and the Croatian authorities tried to disenfranchise them and disarm them. You've explained that to us. Now, tell us this, please: Do you happen to know that anybody had proclaimed or established some sort of Dubrovnik Republic or wanted to cleanse it of any Serb -- of the Serb population?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Non-Serb, non-Serb population, interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What do you know about the Dubrovnik Republic?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, for the benefit of the Trial Chamber - perhaps they don't know about this - but the Dubrovnik Republic was something that existed over the centuries on the territory of the town of Dubrovnik and its immediate environment as a trading town and a trading republic which managed to keep its independence of the Turkish Ottoman Empire that had ruled in the Balkans for 500 years and to be independent of Venice as well, the Venetian Republic, which was across the water, across the Adriatic, and a superpower at the time. Now the idea of the existence of a Dubrovnik Republic I know about only on the basis of what I was able to read in the newspapers, and I learnt a lot more about it when I withdrew from political life from a documentary, in fact, that was filmed by the Belgrade company Akitel [phoen], and it showed a meeting of citizens, an Assembly of citizens from the Cavtat and Dubrovnik area and it was held in the Croatia Hotel in Cavtat, and the author of that idea, who expounded the concept at that meeting, was an eminent citizen of Dubrovnik. I don't know what he was ethnically speaking, was he a Croat or an Italian, but his name was Aleksandar Apolonio, and for a long period of time he was -- he occupied prominent functions in the court system and the prosecutor's office for Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did any Serb factor have a part to play in any -- in this story about some kind of Dubrovnik Republic? And more specifically in that general story about the Dubrovnik Republic, was the idea tenable to do away with non-Serb -- the non-Serb population from the Dubrovnik area? Would that have been feasible?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nobody, as far as I know, none of the Serbs had any influence on this, wielded any influence or was included in that process at all, and I think the idea that the aim was to do away with the Croatian and non-Serb population in the area was quite nonsensical, absurd.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Could -- could we say that the JNA in any way, directly or indirectly, participated in the planning, designing, or executing this removal of non-Serb population from the Dubrovnik Republic, SAO Krajina, SAO Western Slavonia, and so on and so forth?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can say with full responsibility that the JNA never played any such role, particularly about Dubrovnik. That's where it's most evident. No matter how much torchings there were in those areas where the JNA passed through and where it was attacked, you have the town of Cavtat. The entire Cavtat remained completely intact, with not a single bullet fired. The only thing damaged was Croatia Hotel, which was the seat, the base of Croat paramilitary units. Otherwise, the town was defended without a single round fired. That means that if in those places where there had been no paramilitary units and where no resistance had been offered to the Yugoslav People's Army as the only legitimate armed force, there was no torching and no damage.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What was the relationship between the JNA and the Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already said that in the circumstances of the immediate threat of war, Territorial Defence directly subordinates to JNA units because they join the JNA and fall under their command and control.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. You mentioned one order by the Presidency. That means that the Territorial Defence was part of the defence, both in peace and in war, but you have one order of the Presidency from December 1991 that refers to volunteers. Tab 50. What was the purpose of issuing this order? It says "Vice-president Branko Kostic."

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is an order issued by the SFRY Presidency on the 20th of December, 1991. This order was designed to reconfirm once again something that had already been settled in various pieces of legislation, including the law on national defence. It says that: "Pursuant to the provisions of Article 119 of the Law on All People's Defence, in circumstances of immediate threat of war, the Territorial Defence and the Yugoslav People's Army shall be reinforced also with volunteers ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You don't need to dwell on this, but at the very outset you said that this is an order to engage volunteers in the armed forces of the SFRY during an imminent threat of war.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In item 5, it says: "A volunteer who joins a unit or institution of the armed forces of the SFRY ... becomes a military man, wears the uniform and the standard insignia of the members of the armed forces of the SFRY and shall have all the other rights and duties pertaining to persons serving in the armed forces of the SFRY." Can this in any way be qualified as an irregularity, as forming paramilitary units that the Presidency would have been doing by issuing this order?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. All this was very clearly regulated by the law on national defence. This order recalls once again and obligates military commands to honour those provisions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Look at 26(e) on the Croatian indictment. It says -- sorry, 26(g): "exerted effective control or substantial influence over the JNA ..." et cetera, et cetera. Is there anything that I did, anything in the legislation apart from this order regulating the joining up of the volunteers?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know of the existence of any such thing, but if I may say so, adopting legislation was not even in your purview. Not only your purview, it was not even in the purview of the SFRY Presidency. Legislation was normally adopted by the federal parliament as proposed by the federal government.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, I just note that paragraph (g) speaks of exerting effective control. This speaks to de facto control, not necessarily de jure control. So speaking of legislation, or confining the answer to legislation will not necessarily deal with the allegation made.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Robinson, but in 26(i), if it says: "effectively ordered the passage of laws ..." then those laws should exist. It means that I illegally ordered the adoption of some laws which were then supposedly adopted, but such laws does not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] (I). I am talking about paragraph (i), which says: "effectively ordered the passage of laws and regulations ..."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I thought you were referring to paragraph (g). I think that's what was said.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. We can take (g): "exerted effective control or substantial influence over the JNA which participated in the planning, preparation and execution of the forcible removal of the Croat and other non-Serb population from the SAO ..." and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Please, Professor Kostic, what kind of effective control did I have over the JNA? It's true that we have already gone through the testimony of General Vasiljevic, but let us go back to this: What kind of effective control did I exert on the JNA?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really know nothing about that. I said a moment ago if General Vasiljevic as Prosecution witness produced allegations of that kind, and in view of the nature of his job, he was in a much better position to know about such things than I was, I can only say that I completely agree with what Mr. Vasiljevic said, and I really think -- think that you had no control over the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Okay. Let us look at things from another angle. The Presidency of the SFRY and you as the president --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Vice-president.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, vice-president, but also the chairman in one period. Throughout this period that is relevant, from before the 1st of August until June 1992, did you have information about engagements of the JNA? Did you receive briefings from the Supreme Command Staff, the General Staff, et cetera? At least regarding major engagements of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we did receive such information. We as members of the Presidency frequently -- frequently toured the war zones where we received briefings about the situation, but I must say you didn't attend any such meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. I didn't attend. But did any of these activities of the JNA directly or indirectly have anything to do with my influence? You knew about all those activities, so you must have been aware, I suppose, if those activities were linked to me in any way.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But you knew about all the activities of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And you cannot link any one of them to me?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, let us go back to subparagraph (i): "effectively ordered the passage of laws and regulations ..." Were any laws and regulations adopted?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Regarding Dubrovnik and the engagement of JNA?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. In that period, no. We had the existing constitution from before, the law on the national defence, and there was this order that was issued by the Presidency in its role of Supreme Command. But there was no new legislation in that period.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, tell me, under the constitution and all the other legislation, as well as de facto in practice, how did the Assembly and the federal government operate at that time? Who did these bodies consist of? How did they operate? Who led them?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time, the federal parliament had two Chambers; the Chamber of Republics and the Chamber of Representatives. The Chamber of Republics consisted of representatives of all republics and autonomous provinces, and the Federal Chamber was made up according to a different principle. The principle "one citizen, one vote" was adjusted, and every republic had a limited number of representatives. There could be a limited number of representatives coming from one and the same republic. The federal government was led by Prime Minister Ante Markovic from Croatia. It consisted of men from -- people from all republics, but I must say that already at this period the regularity of work in the parliament and in the government were deeply upset, because various republics started withdrawing their representatives, both from the parliament and the government.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Stop there. The federal parliament was particularly paralysed already in December 1991.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Ante Markovic resigned from his job because he didn't agree with the proposed budget in December 1991. Under those circumstances, the Presidency would have been entitled to issue decisions with the force of law.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you adopt any decision with the force of law, and did you exercise this right to perform a partly governmental function?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already said that the Presidency of the SFRY, beginning with the 3rd October, 1991, when it began operating under circumstances of immediate threat of war in a reduced composition, had a constitutional right to adopt decrees with the force of law. However, throughout its existence, it never issued any such decree, either in terms of passing legislation or in terms of limiting the existing amount of political freedoms, the operation of political parties, the operation of political and party leaderships elected at multi-party, free elections.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How about assistance and support to the JNA within its constitutional powers? Is that some sort of illegal activity?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a completely legal activity based on laws and the constitution of the SFRY.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Subparagraph (j) says: "directed, commanded, controlled, or otherwise provided substantial assistance or support to the JNA, the Serb-run TO staff, and volunteer forces deployed in the --" and then it goes on to enumerate all these districts, ending with the Dubrovnik Republic - "in the execution of the purpose of the joint criminal enterprise ..." Can you say, did I really direct and command and control all these JNA forces, the Territorial Defence, and volunteer units?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that allegation is untrue, just as the allegation that the JNA was Serb run. Even in 1992, both in the general staff, that is the Supreme Command Staff, and in many units of the Yugoslav People's Army from the highest to the lowest level, we had members of other Yugoslav ethnicities who remained serving on the command and in the units of the JNA. The only difference was that the inflow of new recruits, new conscripts, was considerably reduced, and this indictment practically accuses both you and us in the Presidency of Serbicising the army. The reality is that this was a result of the secessionist behaviour of certain republics, which violated their constitutional obligation to send their conscripts to the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You put it very mildly. Let us look now at a video, because this story about the Dubrovnik Republic -- I won't finish this sentence. Let us see this video. It's ready.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "[Voiceover] And presented the idea about the establishment of the Dubrovnik Republic. It is a small party movement which wishes to rally all the citizens of Dubrovnik and those who are dispersed all over the world in a common aspiration to create a demilitarised autonomous unit. In other words, the Republic of Dubrovnik."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: This is something different now. Is this the person which -- who you said you didn't know whether he was a Croat or an Italian, Apolonio?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's Aleksandar Apolonio.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor Kostic. In the same paragraph, subparagraph (k), it says: "directed, commanded, controlled or otherwise provided substantial assistance or support to the police forces within the MUP of the Republic of Serbia, including the DB, whose members assisted in the execution of the purpose of the joint criminal enterprise ..." and then goes on, the enumeration of all these districts, ending with the Dubrovnik Republic. For as long as you were a member of the Presidency, did the MUP pursue the aim of some joint criminal enterprise anywhere?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that, and I know for a fact that the MUP of Serbia had absolutely no involvement or influence in the Dubrovnik operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What do you know about this: Did the army or the police in Krajina perpetrate any crimes? When I say "police," I mean the police force of Krajina. And when I say "the army," I mean the JNA and the Territorial Defence of Krajina. Are you aware that the army and the police committed any crimes there?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would be telling less than the complete truth if I answered no. I'm not aware that they committed crimes, but I don't rule out the possibility. It was a civil war, and I don't rule out the possibility that on all sides in that civil war there were individuals who perpetrated crimes. And throughout my testimony, even though I refuted many allegations in the indictment, I don't want to be understood as supporting any crime. I am indeed in favour of punishing all serious crimes in the harshest way, but I don't want individuals or groups accused lightly or accusing one side only. But there is a certainty that crimes were committed on all sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know who committed crimes on the Serb side?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't tell you precisely at this moment because I didn't have data about those individual crimes that were happening at the time. I can only say that later, when I retired from political life in mid-1992 and while following the work of this Tribunal, which I did very carefully, as often as I could, I found out that in most cases it was paramilitary units.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. And what was the attitude of the authorities in Serbia and Yugoslavia and also in the Krajinas toward the crimes perpetrated by paramilitary groups or paramilitary formations or whatever you want to call them?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can only say that we in the Presidency of the SFRY had occasion more than once to issue warnings and to draw attention to this. We were informed by the competent authorities in the staff of the Supreme Command that all these individual crimes were being dealt with, that the perpetrators were being tried and severely punished, but I cannot give you any specific examples. I know, for example, when I was in Knin as president of the state commission, on the same day when Bogicevic and Tupurkovski went to see Tudjman in Zagreb based on our joint agreement in the commission, I was told that there were indeed Serbs in Knin who had violated the law and who were in detention there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: It was then that you were informed that individual Serbs had been arrested for perpetrating crimes, when you were there?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Professor, earlier you said that you found out that in most cases where these crimes had been committed on the Serb side, you said it was mostly paramilitary units. Can I ask what you meant by "paramilitary units" on the Serb side. Could you clarify.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To be quite precise and clear, I said that while I was performing the duty of deputy president, I did not have much information about the individual crimes that had been perpetrated - I've already said this - but that after I retired from political life, after June 1992, I had occasion to hear through the media, and especially following the trials before this Tribunal, that paramilitary formations had committed crimes. So I can only tell you what you have already heard here. There was mention of the White Eagles, Dusan Silni, and so on and so forth. These were paramilitaries units which were not part of the JNA and the Territorial Defence and the volunteers who joined the JNA.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 29 of the Croatia indictment, it says: "Slobodan Milosevic, while holding positions of superior authority, is also individually criminally responsible for the acts or omissions of his subordinates ..." and so on and so forth. It goes on to say that: "A superior is responsible for the criminal acts of his subordinates if he knew or had reason to know that the subordinates were about to commit such acts or had done so ..." What post was I holding at the relevant time? This alleged joint criminal enterprise is said to have started before the 1st of August until the end of June 1992.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, you were the President of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And who were my subordinates at that time?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would be very difficult for me to name them right now in view of the fact that both in Serbia and in all the other Yugoslav republics power was divided into the three branches of government; the executive, the judiciary, and the legislative branch. No one can deny that as president of Serbia, you had undoubtedly the greatest political authority and influence. Since you're asking me about it, I would expect Mr. Nice to issue an indictment tomorrow against Mr. Blair, for example, for all the murders and the rapes and the robberies that had occurred in London the previous night, for example.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: At that time, you were in Belgrade very often. Among the persons who were my subordinates, can any of them be said to have participated in crimes in Bosnia or Croatia?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now I have to go on to paragraph 30 concerning you and others, which reads as follows: "From at least March 1991 until the 15th of June, 1992, Slobodan Milosevic exercised control over the four members of the 'Serbian Bloc' within the Presidency of the SFRY. These four individuals are Borisav Jovic, the representative of the Republic of Serbia; Branko Kostic, the representative of the Republic of Montenegro; Jugoslav Kostic, the representative of the autonomous province of Vojvodina; Sejdo Bajramovic, the representative of the autonomous province of Kosovo and Metohija. Slobodan Milosevic used Borisav Jovic and Branko Kostic as his primary agents in the Presidency, and through them, he directed the actions of the 'Serbian Bloc.' From the 1st of October 1991, in the absence of the representatives of the Presidency from Croatia, Slovenia, Macedonia and Bosnia-Herzegovina, the four members of the 'Serbian Bloc' exercised the powers of the Presidency, including that of collective 'Commander-in-Chief' of the JNA. This 'Rump Presidency' acted without dissension to execute Slobodan Milosevic's policies. The Federal Presidency had effective control over the JNA as its 'Commander-in-Chief' and the TO units and the volunteer units acting in coordination and under supervision of the JNA. Generals Veljko Kadijevic and Blagoje Adzic, who directed and supervised the JNA forces in Croatia, were in constant communication and consultation with the accused." Can these four enumerated members of the Presidency be called the Serbian Bloc?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I've already answered that. First of all, I come from Montenegro, and I always declare myself as a Montenegrin. Although Montenegro is a small country, the Prosecution, to be precise, should have said the Serbian and Montenegrin Bloc. Secondly, throughout the indictment the Prosecution uses the term "the Serbian Bloc" in a pejorative way. Had it wanted to be consistently objective, it should have spoken of the advocates of secession from and the break-up of Yugoslavia and those who advocated the preservation of Yugoslavia. Instead, they used the term "the Serbian Bloc." That's why I say that they are practically plagiarising Mr. Mesic's book. But Mr. Mesic calls us "the gang of four."

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, these comments of the witness are absolutely inappropriate here. He's commenting constantly that we are actually more or less writing from Mr. Mesic's book. I mean, that's absolutely inappropriate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'm not sure that I agree. To say that you are plagiarising a book, that's not offensive. It's either that it is or it isn't. But rather than concentrating, Mr. Milosevic, on the nomenclature "Serbian Bloc," which is just a name, why don't you focus the witness's attention on what it is alleged that these four people did? That seems to me to be the important allegation, not the name.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We won't go into the name.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What crime did you, as the Serbian Bloc or as the Presidency, commit? What decision did you issue, even with the best of intentions, which had tragic consequences or led to loss of human life, material damage and such like?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my testimony so far, I said that the Presidency of the SFRY, either in its full or reduced composition, issued no decision that might be described as a joint criminal enterprise. When asked by Mr. Robinson, I also said that I don't even know a single decision that might have inflamed the conflict and influenced developments in such a way as to lead to escalation of war and inter-ethnic conflict. Unless I am interrupted by the Prosecution, I expect Mr. Nice and his associates to present some such criminal decision as none of these are mentioned in the indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, it's time for the break. We will adjourn for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Professor Kostic, did I use Borisav Jovic and you as my main agents in the Presidency of the SFRY and direct the actions of the Serb Bloc through you, as stated in the paragraph that I quoted to you?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, for the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can assert that you did not use me for those purposes. I can only assume that you had more frequent communications with Mr. Jovic than you had with me because he was representing Serbia in the Presidency. But even had you had such absolute control over us, I've just stated that there is not a single decision issued by that Presidency which might represent a criminal enterprise or instigate someone else to commit a crime.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: To whom were you yourself responsible?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was responsible to the Assembly of Montenegro, although the mandate of members of the Presidency was not of such a nature as to represent an imperative. In other words, it was not the duty of members of the Presidency to necessarily comply with the decisions of their own republican Assemblies. However, we did consult on all important issues. I consulted my republican Assembly on every important issue, and they could have replaced me at any moment had they assessed my work as not adhering to what the Assembly felt should be done.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Could you comment on the part of the rather long quotation which I read out to you that the Federal Presidency had effective control over the JNA, over the TO and volunteer units which were acting in a coordinated manner under the supervision of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All I can say is that this is one of the few correct statements in this indictment. It's true that the Presidency was the civilian Supreme Command of the armed forces. Apart from the JNA, those armed forces comprised the police force, the Territorial Defence and volunteers. Therefore, the Presidency did control the JNA, although the immediate operative command and control was within the purview of the General Staff as a professional organ. In this period in particular, while we were operating as a reduced Presidency, most of our decisions had to do with cease-fire agreements, authorising Mr. Veljko Kadijevic as responsible for these matters as he was the minister of defence and was the superior of the General Staff and the Supreme Staff -- Command to negotiate these cease-fires, and we could verify whether he had acted in compliance with our instructions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And what did you establish in your working relations with the General Staff? Did Kadijevic indeed comply with your instructions?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only in one case was there a disagreement. At one of these peace negotiations, and I think it was on the 10th of October in The Hague, if I'm correct, the Croatian mass media, and I think Mr. Hans Van den Broek, stated that Veljko Kadijevic had agreed for the whole JNA to pull out of Croatia. Of course he had not agreed to that, and he said that he was not competent to do that. We discussed this at the Presidency, and the Presidency adopted a categorical standpoint which was identical to that of Mr. Kadijevic, to the effect that the JNA could not withdraw from the flashpoints in Croatia until another solution was found to provide physical security for the Serb population on the territories of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I will not continue to quote from this because we've already dealt with my alleged influence on Kadijevic and others, and Vasiljevic testified about this here. So please look at paragraph 31 of the Croatia indictment, which reads: "Slobodan Milosevic exercised effective control over KOS, the counter-intelligence component of the JNA. His control over the leaders of KOS, particularly over General Aleksandar Vasiljevic, enabled the engagement of KOS agents in Croatia. Agents of the KOS carried out the policies of Slobodan Milosevic in Croatia by directing the actions of local Croatian Serb political leaders, directing and supporting the local Serb police and security forces, and introducing Serb volunteer groups into Croatia and supporting their activities." Now, please tell me whether I had any de facto control over Vasiljevic or KOS.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that you had any control over Vasiljevic, and I can say that I as the vice-president of the Yugoslav state Presidency and member of that Supreme Command, I did not have direct control over Vasiljevic either. According to the rules of service and the way in which communication was regulated, the head of the 12th KOS administration was directly responsible to the Federal Secretary for National Defence, that is to say Mr. Veljko Kadijevic. So that what I can say is that with the exception of the several meetings that I had with Mr. Aleksandar Vasiljevic in the war office of the staff of the Supreme Command, where as the Supreme Command we were present there, the most responsible people of the Supreme Command were there and to tell them of the situation. So apart from those meetings, I can say that not even I had a single meeting with Mr. Vasiljevic as a tete-a-tete meeting, alone with him one-on-one. And I don't know that you ever did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Of course I didn't. And that's -- and not even Vasiljevic himself as a Prosecution witness said that here. But tell me, since when did the KOS -- was the KOS operational on the territory of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't really give you an exact date. I think that KOS as a service, intelligence service in the Yugoslav People's Army -- I don't know if it changed names, but KOS was active on the territory of Croatia, as it was indeed on all other parts of Yugoslav territory within a united SFRY as part and parcel of the corresponding service of the JNA since 1945 onwards, until the 27th of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Was it active on the territory of Serbia and Montenegro and in fact throughout the territory of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Well, I've just said so. It was active in all the republics all over the territory of Yugoslavia; on the territory of Croatia as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you know anything about the allegation made here that KOS -- agents of the KOS carried out the policies in Croatia by directing the actions of local Croatian Serb political leaders, directing and supporting the local Serb police and security forces and so on?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And did KOS agents bring in -- introduce Serb volunteer groups in Croatia and support their activities?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never heard about anything like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Paragraphs 34 and 35 run as follows: "From on or about the 1st of August, 1991 until June 1992 ..." Is that the time that you were vice-president of the Presidency?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, it says here "... Slobodan Milosevic, acting alone or in concert with other known and unknown members --" et cetera, et cetera -- "of the joint criminal enterprise planned, instigated, ordered, committed or otherwise aided and abetted the planning, preparation or execution of the persecution of the Croat and other non-Serb civilian population" from all these territories. And then paragraph 35 says: "Throughout this period, Serb forces, comprised of JNA units, local TO units, and TO units from Serbia and Montenegro, local and Serbian MUP police forces -- police units and paramilitary units, attacked and took control of towns, villages and settlements in these territories listed above. After the takeover, the Serb forces, in cooperation with the local Serb authorities, established a regime of persecutions designed to drive the Croat and other non-Serb civilian population from these territories."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, in relation to paragraph 34, don't ask the witness whether you, acting alone or in concert with other members of a joint criminal enterprise, committed the crimes set out. That's -- that's the kind of general question to which the kind of answer that this witness gives and has given in the past will not be helpful. In relation to paragraph 35, you can ask him about the issues of fact that are raised therein.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, I will follow what you said, but don't forget that the witness was quoted as one of those who allegedly, together with me, committed what it says in paragraph 34. And if that were true, he would have to know about something like that. And in paragraph 35, it says "Serb forces comprised of JNA units." Now, were the JNA units Serb forces?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. They were Yugoslav forces, Yugoslav armed forces of the SFRY.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Were all the other units subordinate to the JNA units, the TO and all the others listed here?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Territorial Defence and the volunteers were subordinated to the JNA units, and the police forces as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Was the JNA at the head of those units or, rather, did it ever attack or take control -- attack and take control of towns, villages, and settlements, and after that did it drive the Croat and other non-Serb civilian population from these territories?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those are unsubstantiated facts. The fact is that the JNA army, Yugoslav People's Army, in many towns and barracks in Croatia at that point in time was under siege all the time. It was blocked all the time. So it was not able even to move around anywhere, even when they had to pull out those units from the barracks in other parts of Yugoslavia. And secondly, it's a great untruth, a major untruth to claim that the Yugoslav People's Army in any case or event whatsoever organised or attempted to effect the forcible transportation of civilians from any parts. The JNA was neutral at all times, until the point in time when the Croatian paramilitary formations had become so strong that they began to launch direct attacks against the JNA itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: These persecutions, according to paragraph 36, comprised of the killing or displacement of several thousands of civilians and the incarceration of civilians, thousands, and the establishment and perpetuation of inhumane living conditions for Croat and other non-Serb civilian detainees within the mentioned detention facilities. And then it goes on to talk about the unlawful attacks on Dubrovnik and undefended Croat villages, the beating and robbing of Croat and other non-Serb civilians, and so on and so forth. Now, do you have any knowledge about any of these activities alleged in the indictment? Is there anything there that you can say is correct from all the elements that I have read out?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no knowledge about any of that, and the idea that is -- is a thread through the whole indictment, I can say that it is completely unfounded to claim that the Yugoslav People's Army expelled or displaced en masse or even killed and incarcerated people. What I know for sure, for certain, is that the Yugoslav People's Army, in a situation where it had been attacked itself and was placed in a position to have to defend itself, that's what happened. It was an inter-ethnic conflict, a civil war throughout the territory of Croatia at the time, and it is quite certain and common knowledge that there were armed civilians over there as well, that is to say armed citizens, and that in those clashes and conflicts there were people who had been taken prisoner, and those people had to be put up somewhere, accommodated somewhere, gathered together somewhere until their fate had been decided. And for the benefit of the Trial Chamber, I can say that Vukovar, for example, which is mentioned most frequently -- may I be allowed to finish my line of thought, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Vesna Bosanac, I think she was the director, for example, of the Vukovar Hospital. She was one of the persons who were detained in Vukovar, for example, by the Yugoslav People's Army, held in custody. And on the basis of a full court decision, on the basis of an investigation, Ms. Vesna Bosanac was proclaimed a war criminal. Later on, she was exchanged on the principle of one for all, all for one, all for all on the basis --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- basis of an agreement. May I be allowed to finish what I was saying?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No. I'm not being helped by the answer, and I'm going say what I said before, Mr. Milosevic: This line of questioning is not helpful. If you look at 36(a), it sets out the grounds for the allegation of persecutions, and then it finishes by saying: "... as described in detail in paragraphs 38 to 59 and 73 to 75," and the allegation in (b) is also "... as described in detail in paragraph 64." So referring the witness to these general allegations and having him say no is not helpful to the Court. You would be much better advised to deal with the specific allegations of crimes that are set out in the indictment if the witness has evidence to give in relation to them.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Very specifically now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let me make it clear. I'm not inviting you -- I'm not inviting you to go through the indictment paragraph by paragraph. I'm merely indicating that the line of questioning that you're pursuing is not helpful to you or to the Court. And this witness has been here for several days now, and you must be concluding shortly, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I'm doing my best to conclude as shortly as possible, get through the questions as quickly as possible, but there are a lot of them, and this person was president of the Yugoslav state Presidency, which was the supreme command of the JNA at that material time, and it is claimed here that they were all subordinate to the JNA, and he as the president of that body had to be better informed than me about what was going on. And if he doesn't know something, how am I supposed to know it? Because the Presidency of the SFRY was in charge and in control throughout the territory of Yugoslavia. My competence and authority stretched to the territory of Serbia alone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let us proceed and bring this witness's examination-in-chief to a conclusion as quickly as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Professor Kostic, let's take paragraph 64 and 65 of the Croatia indictment, for example, which speak about incarceration contrary to the law, and so on and so forth. So let's see what it says here. Mr. Robinson has told us to be concrete, specific. This is what it says: "Serb military forces, comprised of JNA, TO and volunteer units, acting in cooperation with local and Serbian police staff and local Serb authorities, arrested and detained thousands of Croat and other non-Serb civilians from the territories specified in the following short- and long-term detention facilities." So let's take a look at those detention facilities and see what they are. First of all, it says "Serb military forces comprised of the JNA." Can they be referred to as Serb military forces in that 1991 and 1992?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It was the Yugoslav People's Army. They were the armed forces of the SFRY.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Right. Now, take a look at the following: You have specifically listed here from (a) to (q): "Military warehouse in Morinje in Montenegro, run by the JNA, approximately 320 detainees."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, establish first the foundation for the answer that the witness will give. How would he have been in a position to know about these detention facilities and whether the activities alleged actually took place. Elicit from him evidence as to those matters first.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Professor Kostic, you said a moment ago that your confident -- competence was the effective control of the JNA; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, in this paragraph 64, we have a list of exclusively JNA facilities. There are no other facilities apart from the JNA facilities listed. Now, on the basis of that, am I to conclude that if somebody knew about that at the top political echelons and it had to do with the JNA, it would have had to have been you.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That would have been normal, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, tell us, please, what you know about the fact that in Montenegro, your very own republic, in the military barracks -- or warehouse, rather, of the JNA, there were 320 detainees. What do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, my answer to that question will be the same answer to all the other facilities mentioned. And I have to tell you that I am really not in a position to know about it. I didn't know about it then; I didn't -- don't know about it now, which facilities they were, how many detainees there were in them, and so on. But as to what is alleged and listed in the indictment, you could only draw one conclusion, and that is that everything stated in the indictment leads to the conclusion that we're dealing with military facilities, that is to say facilities of the Yugoslav People's Army, belonging to them. So those facilities of the Yugoslav People's Army were used by the Yugoslav People's Army and the armed forces of the SFRY in order to gather together and accommodate the prisoners of war or detainees or whatever you like to call them, after which those detainees were treated according to the Geneva Conventions, as far as I know. And a moment ago when I mentioned Mrs. Vesna Bosanac, although she was convicted as a war criminal, she was still alive, she was exchanged. In other words, the Yugoslav People's Army and its command, the command of the armed forces, did not commit any crimes towards those detainees. Now, how many of them there were and where the facilities were, I really can't say. I don't know. It wasn't my duty to know either. And that is why at one point I said that Mr. Nice could probably indict Mr. Blair, for example, for many crimes that happened last night in London, for example.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Here in several places -- well, I'm going to skip over some of the specific concrete locations that are not in Serbia, but under (d), it says the agriculture farm of the JNA in Stajicevo, Serbia, then the military barracks in Zrenjanin in Serbia, then the military barracks in Begejci in Serbia, then the military barracks in Zrenjanin in Serbia, then the military prison in Sremska Mitrovica, which is Serbia again, and then the military prison in Sid in Serbia, and I think I have mentioned all the facilities in Serbia. They were all military facilities or, rather, JNA facilities, ranging from barracks to military prisons. Now, tell me, please, as the vice-president of the Yugoslav state Presidency and a Yugoslav politician who was well acquainted with the situation at the time and the provisions that prevailed at the time, did the Republic of Serbia have any competence and authority over the JNA facilities on its territory?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. Neither the Republic of Serbia or any other republic had any powers over military installations on their respective territories. For instance, there was a military hotel in Kupari, and it was not the Croatian authorities that had control over it but the JNA. The regulations were such --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You have answered the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. You said a moment ago that you neither knew nor you were able to know in which locations the JNA held prisoners taken captive during these conflicts. So if neither you nor the JNA were in a position to know that, how could I have known, as President of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Don't answer that. Don't answer that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: It is alleged here that in these prisons mentioned in paragraph 65, the living conditions in the detention facilities were brutal and characterised by inhumane treatment, overcrowding, starvation, and constant physical and psychological assault, including mock executions, torture, beatings, and sexual assault. Do you know anything about this? The reference is to JNA facilities --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... does know anything, and if he does know anything, Mr. Milosevic, what is the source? What is the basis for this knowledge? That's the only way we'll be able to assess the weight to be attached to his evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you ever have, directly or indirectly, officially or unofficially, any information about sexual assaults, torture in those places of detention where prisoners taken by the JNA were held?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never. But I cannot rule out the possibilities that individuals behaved inhumanely, although I personally never had such information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Kostic, how many of these installations did you actually visit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] None. I never visited any such facility. In that period, I made two tours, once to Bacin Bajinska [phoen] --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You've answered my question. In light of that, it seems to me this current line of inquiry is pointless.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Professor Kostic, you say you never visited any of these JNA facilities. Would I have been expected, as President of Serbia, to go around visiting JNA facilities?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. There were absolutely no grounds for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Paragraph 67 of the Croatia indictment refers to forcible transfer of Croats and other non-Serb civilian population in the territories of all the various SAOs and the Dubrovnik Republic. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can say with full responsibility that it is completely incorrect.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Concerning the method of these deportations, we can read about that in paragraph 68 and 69. It says this was done to -- it was done by "... 'White Eagles,' 'Seselj's men,'... 'Arkan's Tigers,' in cooperation with police units, including 'Martic's Police,' SNB -" I don't know what SNB is supposed to mean - "and the Serbian MUP, and others under the effective control of Slobodan Milosevic or other participants in the joint criminal enterprise. They surrounded Croat towns and villages and demanded the inhabitants to surrender their weapons, including legally owned hunting rifles. Then, the towns and villages were attacked, even when those inhabitants had complied with the demands. These attacks were intended to compel the population to flee. After taking control of the towns and villages, the Serb forces sometimes rounded up the remaining Croat and other non-Serb civilian population and forcibly transported them to locations in Croatia controlled by the Croatian government or deported them to locations outside Croatia, in particular Serbia and Montenegro. On other occasions, the Serb forces in cooperation with the local Serb authorities imposed restrictive and discriminatory measures on the non-Serb population and engaged in a campaign of terror designed to drive them out of the territory." The majority of them was forcibly transferred --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff, in the Prosecution case did you lead evidence identifying the towns and villages --

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, we did. We actually did. We had in particular here Colonel Grujic who gave all the details on which -- in which villages population was moved out. It was in particular he who gave all the numbers, the figures on which people were taken out where.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Can you just give me the names of one or two of those?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Villages?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Because that is what Mr. Milosevic should be concentrating on.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: It's actually --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Not the general question to which he'll get a general answer. He should be asking the witness about the particular towns or villages that were mentioned in the Prosecution case.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's the same villages that are actually mentioned in paragraph 36(a). When you look at the locations, these are actually also the locations where the people were expelled.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff. It seems to me that's what you should be directing the witness's attention to, if he has evidence about these several villages. He may not have any evidence about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Please, Professor Kostic, there are references to Dalj, Erdut, Klisa, Lovas, Vukovar, Vocin, Bacin, Saborsko, and the surrounding villages: Skabrnja, Nadin, Bruska, Dubrovnik, and environs. At the critical time, the period in the indictment from August 1991 to June 1992, did you have any knowledge about these misdeeds allegedly committed by JNA and local forces?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the majority of the places -- or, rather, about the majority of the places mentioned, I have absolutely no knowledge. I didn't have any then and I don't know anything about them now. All these places are familiar from that period as crisis areas in the territory of Croatia. The only thing I know is about Dubrovnik and the surrounding area. That's the only thing I know well, because during the Dubrovnik operation, I personally toured the units of the JNA in that territory, and I can say with a great degree of certainty that any allegation about deliberate and conscious removal of Croat or non-Serb population from that area is incorrect. I can say for a fact that not only at the time when I visited, but many years later, because most of the JNA members concerned were from Montenegro, I never heard of a single war crime committed during that Dubrovnik operation such as the killing of an old man, a woman, or a child. There was a conflict there between Croatian paramilitary units and the JNA, and there were casualties on both sides. There were people taken prisoner. You mentioned one of the buildings in Boka Kotorska where they were based. I did not visit that place, but I know for a fact that the Yugoslav People's Army, in this difficult and dramatic time, acquitted itself in a humane way with utmost patience that would do honour to every army.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned a number of those places.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Was there JNA presence in any of them?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, those were the places where there had been inter-ethnic conflicts; Erdut, Dalj, and such. In those inter-ethnic conflicts, the army was engaged in order to put a stop to them, to stop them from spreading.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you receive any information about crimes committed in any of these places?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 69, we read: "According to the 1991 census, the Croat and other non-Serb population of these areas was approximately as follows: SAO Krajina: 28 per cent Croats; SAO Western Slavonia 29 per cent Croats; and SAO Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem 47 per cent Croats." And then it goes on to say that the entire Croat population was forcibly removed except for from Dubrovnik Republic as part of the joint criminal enterprise. Do you have any knowledge about these allegations? In your book, on pages 376 to 381, you referred to it. It's tab 72. Your book, I mean.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have already mentioned the most important figures from the 1991 census and 2001 census that indicate how much the share of Croats has grown over the past ten years -- over those ten years in the total population of Croatia and to what extent the number or the share of Serbs is reduced again in the total population. However, it will not hurt if I say that in 1991 in Croatia, the Croat population accounted for 77.9 per cent, whereas in 2001, it accounted for 89.63 per cent. In the same period in Croatia, Serbs accounted for 12.2 per cent in 1991, and in 2001 they accounted for 4.5 per cent. On one of the previous days, I believe it was Judge Bonomy who wanted to know about the ethnic composition of the crisis areas where there was a majority Serb population or where Serbs were a substantial minority. I don't have that data area by area, but if you take as correct the figures from the indictment, and I don't see any reason to doubt that they are correct, then we could conclude that on the territories indicated in the indictment, Croats totaled about 220.000, and there were about 250.000 Serbs. In all of those areas taken together, that is Serb majority areas and Serbs as substantial minority areas. Now, in Serbia, for the same period -- I have figures for 1991. From those figures, we that approximately one-third of the population of Serbia was non-Serb. In other words, out of a total of almost 10 million, which, more precisely, 9.8 million, almost 3.5 million were non-Serbs. I don't have comparable figures, because I don't have separate figures for Kosovo, but what we know is that over the -- those ten years Serbia, together with maybe Montenegro, was the only republic where the number of non-Serbs remained unchanged.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What does that tell us?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it tells us very eloquently that it is nonsensical to claim that anybody - the JNA or the Presidency or the leadership - organised some sort of plan for ethnic cleansing in those areas while at the same time keeping intact the ethnic composition in Serbia itself with such a large number of non-Serb population which was due, among other things, to the large inflow of refugees from Kosovo, Croatia, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In the light of these figures, it seems that when there are large numbers of non-Serbs, nobody touches them, and in those areas where there are few of them, there is a plan to cleanse them.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no explanation for that. It makes no sense.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Can you explain this from paragraph 68: It says that the JNA, TO, and other units surrounded Croat towns and villages, attacked and took over in some areas. And then again in paragraph 108, it says on the 23rd of November, an agreement was concluded by Tudjman, Kadijevic, myself, et cetera, under the aegis of Cyrus Vance. According to that agreement, Croatian authorities were to lift the siege of JNA barracks, and the JNA was to withdraw from Croatia. Now, tell me, if the JNA had -- was it the case that the JNA had surrounded Croatian towns and villages, or was it the case that the JNA itself was under siege in its barracks on the territory of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's a leading question. And we're not getting anywhere with these general questions and general answers, and it's bordering on the abusive, being abusive, Mr. Milosevic, and I'll be paying particular attention to that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, I quoted in order to avoid putting a leading question. I quoted paragraph 108, where it says: "... entered into an agreement under the auspices of ... Cyrus Vance. This agreement called for the lifting of blockades by Croatian forces on JNA barracks and for the withdrawal of JNA forces from Croatia."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What I characterised as a leading question was "Was it the case that the JNA surrounded Croatian towns?" or "It was the case ..." Not only was it, but it was the case that the JNA itself was under siege in its barracks on the territory of Croatia, clearly inviting the latter as the answer. That's leading.
