We're not getting anywhere with these general questions and general answers. It's half past one, and you must bring your examination-in-chief to a conclusion. We are going stop at twenty minutes to two. I expect you to have concluded by that time.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Unfortunately, I cannot finish my examination-in-chief today, Mr. Robinson. I still have quite a few questions for Mr. Kostic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'll have to consult the Chamber as to whether you'll be allowed to continue, because you have been with this witness now for about four days. Continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honours, if the Chamber does decide to allow him to go over into tomorrow, there is about three minutes of administrative matters I'd like an opportunity to deal with at the end of the morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's why I said 1.40, so we'd stop at 1.43. Swiss precision. Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you about paragraph 108, which says that Croatian forces should lift blockades and that JNA forces should withdraw. What I'm asking you is whether it's possible for those who participated and negotiated this agreement, including Tudjman, were so ill-informed that they would write that the JNA should have the siege lifted, whereas in fact it was the JNA that was encircling others, or was the JNA encircled in its barracks and thus encircling others?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's not a proper question and you're doing the same thing; leading. "Or was the JNA encircling its barracks and was encircling others?" And I've told you time and again that merely putting an alternative question to a witness does not take away from its leading character.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And quite apart from that, this witness has dealt with this matter several times already in his evidence. This is entirely repetitive material.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You must conclude by 20 minutes to.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Professor Kostic, was the JNA surrounded in the Croatian towns in which there were barracks?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The JNA was surrounded in all the barracks on the territory of Croatia which had existed there for many years in peacetime. One of our major concerns as the Presidency of the SFRY and the civilian Supreme Command was anxiety for those soldiers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let's move to the next question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I just wanted to remind Mr. Robinson, I think it's very important.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'll skip over what you consider to be too general. Professor Kostic, in paragraph 103 of the so-called Croatia indictment, it says as follows: "Slobodan Milosevic's calls for the union of all Serbs in one state coincided with those agitating for the creation of a 'Greater Serbia.'" I won't quote any further. Did I anywhere call for the creation of a Greater Serbia or for the union of all Serbs in one state?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Never did I hear you issue any such call. I only heard you advocating the preservation of Yugoslavia as a common state in which not only Serbs but also Muslims, Croats, and others could live together.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Please look at tab 51, where something we have already partly quoted is contained. And it also contains my statement of the 16th of March in the Politika of the 17th of March where, among other things, it mentions living in one state, and the year is 1991. Look at the middle of the second paragraph after the first subtitle and see what I say here. I will read it to you, and you can follow, and it can also be placed on the ELMO. "Instead of a democratic federation which should make it possible for the Serbian people together with other Yugoslav people to live in peace in a single state, the anti-Serb coalition is attempting to bring about the dissolution of Yugoslavia ..." What is the state where I say that Serbs live together with other nations in a state?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's the SFRY.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And my advocating the survival of the SFRY, which as I say here should make it possible for the Serb people to live together with other peoples in a joint state on an equal footing and in peace, does this have anything to do with advocating a Greater Serbia, and is it actually a call for Serbs to live in one state?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It has nothing to do with this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Was there already a state in which they were all living together, Muslims, Croats --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You've asked that several times, Mr. Milosevic, and you have the answer you desire.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Advocating the preservation of Yugoslavia, could it have been part of a conspiracy or a joint criminal enterprise?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, you're abusing the process of the Chamber, and I am going to take the exceptional step of terminating the examination-in-chief. We'll hear from Mr. Nice. May I just ask before: Mr. Milosevic, there are some tabs, whether you wish to have the following tendered into evidence: Tabs 77, 64, 71, and 50, and pages 376 to 81 of tab 72. Do you wish to have those admitted?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do, Mr. Robinson, but I have to draw your attention to the fact that I have not asked the witness anything about Bosnia and Herzegovina, and he was in his position until June 1992 as deputy president of the Presidency, until several months after the outbreak of war in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Secondly, in this function, he attended a meeting with Alija Izetbegovic in Skopje where matters were discussed pertaining to the status of the JNA in Bosnia and Herzegovina, which is also of exceptional importance. He was at the top position in Yugoslavia at the time, and Yugoslavia was going through a crisis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, I took the exceptional step of terminating the examination-in-chief because I'd formed the impression that you're deliberately abusing the process of the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not doing that deliberately, Mr. Robinson. If you terminate the examination-in-chief with regard to Croatia, it will no great loss. However, I do have to put some questions with regard to Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Milosevic --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, listen to me. How long will you be in relation to the questions on Bosnia that you have not touched upon, entirely through your own mismanagement of the examination-in-chief?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, before I reply to your question, you have received the witness schedule. I have it here before me in English. Viva voce Branko Kostic, it says 16 hours. That's the envisaged time, and we have used only 12 hours so far according to the records I have just received.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: But you have not used it properly. You haven't used the time properly. How much time will you spend in relation to Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think I can finish in two sessions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, try for one. Mr. Nice, let me hear from you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The only matters that I want to raise do not relate to this witness. One will be in private session, if I have time. May he withdraw and I'll only be a couple of minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Professor, you may leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: While he's withdrawing and we're still in public session, I regret that I shan't be here tomorrow and hope it won't be counted as a discourtesy, and I'm particularly sorry as my learned friend is starting her cross-examination, which I would preferred to hear, of course. Still in public session before we go into private session, while the witness is withdrawing, and noting the rapid conclusion or the advancing conclusion of the accused's allowable time, can I simply respectfully remind the Court that we have yet to deal with timetabling Kristan Bildt [phoen]. Can I remind the accused through the Court that the invitation to him to deal, by agreement, with the issue of the names of the Racak victims is outstanding and hasn't been dealt with, and if it isn't dealt with, is something that we will have to attempt to deal with at the expense of time by rebuttal evidence. So those are the few short matters in public session. With your leave, one minute in private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The tabs that I mentioned will be admitted. We are adjourned until tomorrow, 9.00 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 7th day of February, 2006, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.48 p.m.
